question: Carl Menger's 1871 book launching the Austrian school by founding value on subjective preference was titled:
answer: Principles of Economics
choices: Principles of Economics
Capital and Interest
Human Action
The Theory of Money
context: Published in Vienna alongside Jevons (England) and Walras (Lausanne) — the marginal revolution. Menger taught Crown Prince Rudolf.

question: Carl Menger argued that value comes not from labor or production cost but from:
answer: Subjective individual valuation
choices: Subjective individual valuation
Hours of socially necessary labor
Average cost of production
Land rent flowing upward
context: Menger overturned the classical labor theory. A diamond is worth more than water because each next unit serves a higher-ranked end for the buyer.

question: Ludwig von Mises died on October 10, 1973, in New York at what age?
context: He had outlived the regimes that exiled him from Vienna. His widow Margit established his archive; Rothbard wrote his eulogy.

question: For decades Murray Rothbard ran which famous weekly gathering in his New York living room?
answer: Monday-night seminar
choices: Monday-night seminar
Friday salon
Sunday brunch circle
Wednesday colloquium
context: Future Austrians passed through: Hoppe, Block, Salerno, Joseph Stromberg. Joey, Murray's wife, served coffee. Long arguments ran until dawn.

question: In 1971, Murray Rothbard helped found which political party that he broke with in 1989?
answer: Libertarian Party
choices: Libertarian Party
Constitution Party
Free Soil Party
Reform Party
context: He left over its abandonment of paleo-libertarian roots. Rothbard then helped launch the John Randolph Club with Lew Rockwell and Pat Buchanan allies.

question: Austrian Business Cycle Theory traces booms to what specific cause?
answer: Artificially low interest rates from credit expansion
choices: Artificially low interest rates from credit expansion
Animal spirits driving overinvestment
Real productivity shocks
Coordination failures in expectations
context: When central banks push rates below the time-preference equilibrium, firms over-invest in long-horizon projects. The bust is the necessary correction.

question: Carl Menger argued in 1892 that money emerged through what process — not by decree of any state?
answer: Market evolution from most saleable goods
choices: Market evolution from most saleable goods
State minting from precious metals
Religious sanction of relics
Royal monopoly grants
context: Goods most easily resold — cattle, salt, silver, gold — gradually displaced less saleable ones as media of exchange. Money is a market institution, not a state creation.

question: Money that has value only because the state declares it legal tender for payment of debts is called:
answer: Fiat money
choices: Fiat money
Commodity money
Representative money
Free banking notes
context: From Latin fiat: 'Let it be done'. Every fiat currency in history has either died or radically depreciated. Sound money historically meant gold or silver.

question: Peter Boettke directs the F.A. Hayek Program for Advanced Study in Philosophy, Politics, and Economics at:
answer: George Mason University
choices: George Mason University
Auburn University
Hillsdale College
Grove City College
context: Mason's economics department under Buchanan, then Boettke, became the major academic home of Austrian-public choice synthesis in the US.

question: Friedrich von Wieser's 1889 work systematizing the value theory of the early Austrian school was titled:
answer: Natural Value
choices: Natural Value
Principles of Economics
Capital and Interest
Social Economics
context: Wieser also coined the term 'marginal utility' in German. Less famous than Menger and Bohm-Bawerk, but a major founding figure of the school.

question: Carl Menger, founder of the Austrian school, died in which year, having lived to see Mises's work but not its full impact?
context: Born 1840, died 1921 in Vienna. Mises was 40; the Mises-Kreis was nascent. Menger's son Karl became a noted mathematician at Notre Dame.

question: Friedrich Hayek died in 1992 in which German city where he taught his final years?
answer: Freiburg
choices: Freiburg
Munich
Heidelberg
Berlin
context: He moved to Freiburg from Salzburg in the late 1970s. His son completed editing the Collected Works there. Hayek lived 92 years and 11 days.

question: Elinor Ostrom became the first woman to win the economics Nobel in what year?
context: She shared the prize with Oliver Williamson, the transaction-cost theorist. She died in 2012 at 78. Her commons research drew on Hayek's distributed-knowledge framework.

question: Vernon Smith won the 2002 Nobel for pioneering what method in economics?
answer: Laboratory experiments
choices: Laboratory experiments
Field experiments
Quasi-experimental analysis
Computational simulation
context: Smith trained experimental subjects in classroom markets and found that simple double-auction designs reliably converged to competitive prices — Hayek vindicated.

question: Murray Rothbard's last academic home from 1986 to his death in 1995 was:
answer: UNLV
choices: UNLV
NYU
Brooklyn Polytechnic
Auburn University
context: S.J. Hall University Professor. The Mises Institute moved next to Auburn; Rothbard stayed in Vegas, lecturing to packed rooms of casino workers and seminar students alike.

question: Ludwig von Mises was approximately what age at his death in 1973?
context: Born September 29, 1881, in Lemberg (then Austrian Galicia, now Lviv). He outlived all his Vienna seminar regulars and saw his ideas spread to the next generation.

question: Friedrich Hayek's life span — birth and death — was:
context: Vienna May 8, 1899 to Freiburg March 23, 1992. He lived to see the Berlin Wall fall and the Soviet Union dissolve — vindication of every claim in The Road to Serfdom.

question: Murray Rothbard's life span — birth and death — was:
context: Born March 2, 1926, in the Bronx to Jewish immigrants. Died January 7, 1995, in Manhattan of a heart attack at 68. Joey Rothbard outlived him by years.

question: Carl Menger's life span — birth and death — was:
context: Galician German-speaking lawyer's son. Founder of marginal-utility and subjective-value theory. Died in Vienna at 81, having seen the empire he served collapse.

question: Eugen von Bohm-Bawerk's life span — birth and death — was:
context: Three-time Austrian finance minister, son-in-law of Karl Knies. Died just before WWI. His seminar trained Mises and Schumpeter; the family was on the 100-schilling note.

question: William Easterly's 2006 critique of Western foreign aid was titled:
answer: The White Man's Burden
choices: The White Man's Burden
The Elusive Quest for Growth
The Tyranny of Experts
Reinventing Foreign Aid
context: A former World Bank economist, Easterly accumulated insider evidence that planned development efforts systematically fail. Markets, not aid agencies, lift nations.

question: Adam Smith's 1759 book — written before Wealth of Nations — on sympathy and ethics was titled:
answer: The Theory of Moral Sentiments
choices: The Theory of Moral Sentiments
Wealth of Nations
Lectures on Jurisprudence
An Essay on Astronomy
context: Smith's foundational ethics book. Vernon Smith and Russ Roberts have championed its modern relevance. The two books form one coherent account of human society.

question: Adam Smith published An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations in what landmark year?
context: March 9, 1776 — months before American independence. Smith's central insight: prosperity comes from voluntary exchange driven by self-interest, not from government direction.

question: Murray Rothbard's first published book in 1962 — a treatise that grew from a textbook commission — was titled:
answer: Man, Economy, and State
choices: Man, Economy, and State
America's Great Depression
For a New Liberty
What Has Government Done to Our Money.
context: Henry Hazlitt commissioned a Human Action textbook from young Rothbard. It grew uncontrollably into a 1000-page Austrian magnum opus instead.

question: Ludwig von Mises was born in 1881 in Lemberg, then capital of Austrian Galicia, today known as which city?
answer: Lviv
choices: Lviv
Krakow
Brno
Bratislava
context: His family were assimilated Galician Jews. His brother Richard became a famous mathematician. The town is now in western Ukraine — a borderland between empires.

question: Peter Schiff predicted the 2008 housing crash in real time on CNBC, often using which Austrian framework?
answer: Austrian Business Cycle Theory
choices: Austrian Business Cycle Theory
Real business cycle theory
Marxist crisis theory
Keynesian liquidity trap
context: His 2007 book Crash Proof made the call before the bust. Mainstream pundits laughed; the YouTube highlight reel is one of the great vindications in economics media.

question: Bitcoin's Genesis block, the first block on the chain, was mined on what date?
answer: January 3, 2009
choices: January 3, 2009
October 31, 2008
January 9, 2009
January 12, 2009
context: About 18:15 UTC. Block height 0. Satoshi mined it himself; the 50 BTC subsidy is unspendable due to a quirk of the original code.

question: The 2011-2013 darkmarket that drove Bitcoin's first wave of adoption and attention was called:
answer: Silk Road
choices: Silk Road
AlphaBay
Hansa
Black Market Reloaded
context: Operated by Ross Ulbricht (Dread Pirate Roberts). Shut down October 2013 in an FBI sting at the San Francisco public library. Ulbricht received a double life sentence.

question: Nayib Bukele, Bitcoin's first head-of-state champion, is the president of:
answer: El Salvador
choices: El Salvador
Argentina
Paraguay
Honduras
context: Re-elected in 2024 with around 85% of the vote after dramatically reducing gang violence. His Bitcoin advocacy has made him a global Bitcoin community figure.

question: Bitcoin's protocol targets one new block roughly every:
answer: 10 minutes
choices: 10 minutes
1 minute
1 hour
30 seconds
context: Six blocks an hour, ~144 per day. Six confirmations is the conventional safety margin. The 10-minute interval balances orphan rate against transaction latency.

question: Bitcoin's block subsidy is cut in half roughly every four years, at intervals of exactly:
answer: 210,000 blocks
choices: 210,000 blocks
100,000 blocks
1,000,000 blocks
365,000 blocks
context: Four years times ~52,560 blocks per year. The halvings end around block 6,929,999 (~2140) when the last fractional satoshi is mined.

question: Lightning Network's mainnet launch — and the start of practical real-world Lightning usage — was in:
answer: January 2018
choices: January 2018
February 2015
November 2021
May 2020
context: Lightning Labs released LND v0.4 with mainnet support. Strike, Cash App, Wallet of Satoshi, Phoenix, and Muun followed; tens of millions of channels exist.

question: The maxim warning that coins held on an exchange or custodian are not really yours is:
answer: Not your keys, not your coins
choices: Not your keys, not your coins
Be your own bank.
Verify, don't trust
Stay humble, stack sats
context: Andreas Antonopoulos popularized the phrase. Mt. Gox, QuadrigaCX, Celsius, BlockFi, FTX — each collapse vindicated the maxim. Self-custody is core to Bitcoin's purpose.

question: The first US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds were approved by the SEC on what date?
answer: January 10, 2024
choices: January 10, 2024
October 19, 2021
March 14, 2024
April 19, 2024
context: Eleven funds approved simultaneously, including BlackRock's IBIT, Fidelity's FBTC, and Grayscale's converted GBTC. A defining moment for institutional adoption.

question: Craig Wright's partner Dave Kleiman, whose estate sued Wright over alleged Bitcoin holdings, died in:
context: Kleiman was a Florida forensic-computing expert. The case settled with a jury awarding $100M for breach of partnership but rejecting the Bitcoin-ownership claim.

question: El Salvador in 2021 was the first country to make Bitcoin legal tender; the second was:
answer: Central African Republic (April 2022)
choices: Central African Republic (April 2022)
Argentina (October 2023)
Paraguay (March 2024)
Mexico (June 2022)
context: CAR's legal-tender status was largely symbolic and later quietly reversed. El Salvador remains the primary state-level Bitcoin experiment.

question: Ethereum mainnet launched in:
answer: July 2015
choices: July 2015
January 2014
December 2013
August 2017
context: Vitalik Buterin's white paper appeared in late 2013; the network launched July 30, 2015. Ethereum's pre-sale and foundation structure contrast sharply with Bitcoin's launch.

question: The crypto lending firm that froze withdrawals in mid-2022 and filed for bankruptcy was:
answer: Celsius Network (July 2022)
choices: Celsius Network (July 2022)
BlockFi (November 2022)
Voyager (July 2022)
Genesis (January 2023)
context: Founded by Alex Mashinsky. Used customer deposits in risky DeFi strategies; ran out of liquidity when crypto prices fell. Mashinsky was indicted in 2023.

question: Sam Bankman-Fried was convicted on all seven counts of fraud and conspiracy in:
answer: October 2023
choices: October 2023
March 2024
November 2022
January 2024
context: Jury deliberated under five hours. He was sentenced March 28, 2024 to 25 years in federal prison. Alameda's Caroline Ellison cooperated and received two years.

question: BIP-39 seed phrases are typically how many words long for standard 128-bit entropy wallets?
answer: 12 words
choices: 12 words
8 words
20 words
32 words
context: Standard wallets use 12 or 24 words (128 or 256 bits of entropy). The word list contains exactly 2048 words, each translatable across multiple languages.

question: The BIP-39 standard mnemonic word list contains exactly how many English words?
context: Each word represents 11 bits of entropy. 12 words = 132 bits before checksum. The word lists are also available in Japanese, Spanish, Chinese, French, Italian, Korean, Czech.

question: The US formally defined the dollar in terms of gold through which 1900 law passed under William McKinley?
answer: Gold Standard Act
choices: Gold Standard Act
Federal Reserve Act
Bretton Woods Agreement
Sherman Silver Purchase Act
context: $1 = 23.22 grains of pure gold (~1/20.67 oz). The act ended the bimetallism debate that had roiled politics since the Civil War. Held until 1933.

question: FDR officially revalued the dollar against gold in January 1934 at what new price?
answer: $35 per ounce
choices: $35 per ounce
$50 per ounce
$20.67 per ounce
$100 per ounce
context: A 41% devaluation of the dollar against gold. The Treasury made an enormous one-time bookkeeping profit, which was used to capitalize the Exchange Stabilization Fund.

question: The Lebanese pound, after decades of de facto dollar peg, collapsed in:
context: The Lebanese banking system collapsed; depositors lost most of their savings. The lira lost 98% of its value against the dollar. Hyperinflation and political collapse intertwined.

question: Sri Lanka defaulted on its sovereign debt for the first time in:
context: Following a combination of poor macroeconomic management, the COVID tourism collapse, and chemical-fertilizer ban consequences. Mass protests forced the president's resignation.

question: Gold's 21st century run, from ~$280 in 2000 to ~$2400 by 2024, has been driven primarily by:
answer: Central bank monetary expansion
choices: Central bank monetary expansion
Industrial demand growth
Jewelry demand surge
Mine production decline
context: Volcker-era discipline gave way; QE, ZIRP, and now post-2020 stimulus have driven hard-asset bids. Gold and Bitcoin both serve as escape valves from fiat debasement.

question: The Spanish silver peso that became the global trade currency was called 'pieces of eight' because:
answer: It was scored to break into eight reales.
choices: It was scored to break into eight reales.
Eight were minted per silver bar.
It contained eight grades of silver
It bore eight royal seals
context: The coin's scoring made it convertible into smaller change. The eight-reales coin (the dollar) circulated freely; cutting yielded 'two bits' = a quarter — still slang for 25 cents.

question: The world's second-largest official gold reserve, with around 3350 tons, is held by:
answer: Germany
choices: Germany
France
Italy
China
context: Held by the Bundesbank. Germany repatriated significant portions from New York and Paris in the 2010s — a notable signal about trust in foreign custody.

question: US dimes and quarters ceased to contain meaningful silver under which law?
answer: Coinage Act of 1965
choices: Coinage Act of 1965
Coinage Act of 1873
Federal Reserve Act of 1913
Bretton Woods Agreement
context: Cupronickel sandwiches replaced 90% silver. Silver had been money in the West for thousands of years; the US replaced it under LBJ in less than a century after Bryan's Cross.

question: US one-cent coins ceased to be made of mostly copper and became copper-plated zinc in:
context: When copper prices made the coin's intrinsic value exceed its face. Eisenhower's IKE dollar coins from 1971-78 contained no silver despite their large size.

question: The American Silver Eagle one-ounce silver bullion coin, struck by the US Mint since 1986, has a nominal face value of:
answer: One dollar
choices: One dollar
Twenty dollars
Fifty cents
Ten dollars
context: Absurdly low compared to silver content (~$25-30). The face value preserves legal-tender status. The American Gold Eagle parallels it.

question: The American Gold Eagle bullion coin was first struck by the US Mint in:
context: Authorized under President Reagan, struck from American mined gold. The one-ounce coin's $50 nominal face value bears no relation to its market value of thousands.

question: The first widely traded modern gold bullion coin, introduced in 1967 by South Africa, was the:
answer: Krugerrand
choices: Krugerrand
Maple Leaf
American Eagle
Sovereign
context: Named for Paul Kruger. Used to circumvent apartheid-era export restrictions on raw gold. Canadians introduced the Maple Leaf in 1979; the Americans followed in 1986.

question: The first .9999 fine gold bullion coin, struck by the Royal Canadian Mint starting in 1979, is the:
answer: Canadian Maple Leaf
choices: Canadian Maple Leaf
Australian Kangaroo
Chinese Panda
British Sovereign
context: Set the new purity standard. Subsequent issues moved to .99999. Highly collectible; the bullion-coin market exploded in popularity during the late-1970s gold rush.

question: US paper money issued during the Civil War, not backed by specie, was called:
answer: Greenbacks
choices: Greenbacks
Confederate dollars
Continentals
Silver certificates
context: Issued under the Legal Tender Act of 1862. Lost roughly half their value during the war, then restored to par by 1879. Their constitutionality was upheld 1871.

question: The National Banking Acts of 1863-64 imposed federal standards on banks and:
answer: Taxed state bank notes out of existence
choices: Taxed state bank notes out of existence
Created the Federal Reserve directly.
Suspended the gold standard
Required all dollars be gold-backed.
context: Created a uniform national currency (greenbacks + national bank notes). The 10% tax on state notes effectively ended their circulation. The Federal Reserve came 50 years later.

question: The US suspended dollar convertibility to gold during World War I in:
context: Wartime emergency. Restored quickly after the war. The Federal Reserve, founded 1913, was just beginning to exercise its powers.

question: A famous image from Weimar Germany shows children playing with bricks made of:
answer: Bundled banknotes worthless as money
choices: Bundled banknotes worthless as money
Real bricks marked with prices
Iron Cross medals
Confederate flags
context: When notes became worth less than their wood-pulp paper, they were used as fuel, wallpaper, kite material, and play blocks. The visceral memory passed down generations.

question: Andrew Jackson made his veto of the Second Bank's recharter the central issue of which election?
answer: 1832 presidential election
choices: 1832 presidential election
1828 presidential election
1816 presidential election
1840 presidential election
context: Jackson defeated Henry Clay 219 to 49 in the electoral college. The 'Bank War' is a defining episode in American political history. Jackson's Democrats opposed central banks for generations.

question: The Federal Reserve Act was signed by Woodrow Wilson on what date?
answer: December 23, 1913
choices: December 23, 1913
January 1, 1914
August 15, 1913
November 1, 1913
context: Two days before Christmas, with much of Congress already departed for the holidays. Wilson signed the bill amidst significant procedural controversy. The Fed's foundational moment.

question: Which US president signed the Federal Reserve Act into law in December 1913?
answer: Woodrow Wilson
choices: Woodrow Wilson
William Howard Taft
Theodore Roosevelt
Warren Harding
context: Wilson is reported to have later said: 'I am a most unhappy man. I have unwittingly ruined my country.' The quote is sometimes disputed; the policy was real.

question: Paul Volcker served as Federal Reserve chairman during what years?
context: Appointed by Carter, reappointed by Reagan. Broke the 1970s inflation through high rates. Returned briefly under Obama to lead the Volcker Rule effort restricting bank trading.

question: Alan Greenspan served as Federal Reserve chairman during what years?
context: Initially a Rand-influenced gold standard advocate; in practice he ran an increasingly accommodative monetary policy. Praised as 'Maestro' through 2007; widely criticized after.

question: Bear Stearns, the first major Wall Street firm to collapse in 2008, was sold to JP Morgan with Federal Reserve guarantees in:
answer: March 2008
choices: March 2008
September 2008
October 2008
August 2008
context: Initial price: $2 per share, later raised to $10. The Fed guaranteed $30 billion of Bear's questionable assets. The Bear deal foreshadowed and arguably encouraged Lehman's later defenders.

question: Lehman Brothers, the largest bankruptcy in US history, filed for Chapter 11 on:
answer: September 15, 2008
choices: September 15, 2008
March 14, 2008
October 19, 2008
August 9, 2007
context: Total assets $639 billion. The Fed and Treasury did not bail out Lehman — a still-debated decision. Within 48 hours, the AIG bailout began. Crisis cascade intensified.

question: TARP, the 2008 bank bailout package signed by George W. Bush, authorized initial spending of:
answer: $700 billion
choices: $700 billion
$100 billion
$2 trillion
$300 billion
context: Eventually disbursed less; the program was largely repaid. The political precedent — that Washington would underwrite major bank losses — has shaped expectations ever since.

question: Jerome Powell has served as Federal Reserve chair since:
answer: February 2018
choices: February 2018
January 2014
August 2006
December 2010
context: Appointed by Trump, reappointed by Biden. Initially raised rates and shrank the balance sheet; reversed course in 2020; then engineered the most aggressive tightening cycle since Volcker.

question: By mid-2023, the Federal Reserve had raised the federal funds target range to:
context: The most aggressive tightening cycle since Volcker. Inflation fell back toward 3% range. Critics: the rate destruction of long-duration bonds prefigured Silicon Valley Bank's March 2023 collapse.

question: The European Central Bank was founded in:
answer: June 1998
choices: June 1998
January 1999
December 2008
May 2007
context: Began operations preparing for the euro's January 1, 1999 launch. The ECB's mandate is more narrowly inflation-focused than the Fed's; even so, post-2010 sovereign debt crises forced expansion.

question: The world's oldest still-operating central bank was founded in:
answer: 1694 (Bank of England)
choices: 1694 (Bank of England)
1668 (Sveriges Riksbank)
1791 (First Bank of US)
1800 (Banque de France)
context: Sweden's Riksbank is older. Both originated to fund war debts; the Bank of England's connection to the Glorious Revolution and Treasury credibility set the template followed worldwide.

question: John Maynard Keynes died on what date, just months after Bretton Woods negotiations were complete?
answer: April 21, 1946
choices: April 21, 1946
March 8, 1939
December 1944
January 1947
context: Heart attack at his Sussex country estate. He was 62. His final policy work was the Bretton Woods agreement that institutionalized aspects of his monetary thought.

question: John Hicks's 1937 textbook diagram simplifying Keynes for graduate students was called:
answer: IS-LM model
choices: IS-LM model
AS-AD model
Phillips curve
Mundell-Fleming model
context: Hicks called it a 'translation' of Keynes; later macroeconomists called it a simplification. Hicks himself in 1981 admitted IS-LM had become misleading.

question: Larry Summers's earlier 2013 thesis arguing the US was in chronic low-growth was called:
answer: Secular stagnation
choices: Secular stagnation
Permanent recession
New normal
Zero lower bound
context: Borrowed from Alvin Hansen 1938. The thesis influenced Obama-era policy toward ever-easier money. Summers later changed his diagnosis when 2021 inflation arrived.

question: Georg Friedrich Knapp's 1905 work State Theory of Money — the chartalist starting point — argued money:
answer: Was created by state decree, not market.
choices: Was created by state decree, not market.
Originated as commodity-based exchange
Is a unit of account only.
Has no intrinsic value.
context: Austrian rebuttal: Menger 1892 documented money's market origin in many cultures long predating any state. The Mises-Knapp dispute is foundational for modern monetary debate.

question: Since 2008, the Federal Reserve sets the floor under its policy rate through:
answer: Interest on Reserve Balances (IORB)
choices: Interest on Reserve Balances (IORB)
Discount Window rate
Reserve Requirement Adjustments
Federal Funds Rate alone
context: Pays banks for reserves they hold at the Fed. Eliminates the need for scarce reserves to drive rates. A subtle but important architectural change in monetary plumbing.

question: Jean-Baptiste Say's 'law of markets' is often paraphrased as:
answer: Supply creates its own demand
choices: Supply creates its own demand
Demand drives supply
Markets always clear in equilibrium
Prices adjust instantaneously
context: More carefully: each act of production funds an act of demand by the producer. Keynes attacked it; Austrians defend it, properly understood. Sowell's PhD dissertation explored Say.

question: Adam Smith's first major book, on ethics and sympathy, was published in:
context: Seventeen years before Wealth of Nations. The two books together form Smith's complete account of human society — neither work understood properly in isolation.

question: Karl Marx published volume 1 of Das Kapital in:
context: Hamburg. Bohm-Bawerk's 1896 essay Karl Marx and the Close of His System demolished its central labor theory of value. The book's prophecies have failed without exception.

question: The price at which the quantity buyers wish to buy equals the quantity sellers wish to sell is called the:
answer: Equilibrium price
choices: Equilibrium price
Marginal price
Reservation price
Pareto price
context: Geometrically: where supply and demand curves intersect. Real markets fluctuate around equilibrium continuously; perfect equilibrium is an analytical abstraction.

question: San Francisco's 1994 rent control expansion was studied in 2019 by Diamond, McQuade, and Qian, finding which effect?
answer: Reduced overall rental housing supply
choices: Reduced overall rental housing supply
Increased rental supply
Stable supply but lower rents
No measurable effect
context: Landlords converted controlled units to condos or higher-end uses. Net citywide rent affordability declined. The most rigorous modern study of rent control.

question: In 2019, the first US state to impose statewide rent control was:
answer: Oregon
choices: Oregon
California
New York
New Jersey
context: Statewide caps at CPI + 7%. Followed by California's similar regime. Economists across the political spectrum warned against it; the policies were enacted regardless.

question: John Bogle launched the first low-cost retail index mutual fund — Vanguard's First Index Investment Trust — in:
context: Mocked at the time as 'Bogle's folly'. Today index funds are the dominant retail investment vehicle. A great deflation of Wall Street fees has lifted ordinary savers enormously.

question: A graph of Treasury yields plotted by maturity from 1-month to 30-year is called the:
answer: Yield curve
choices: Yield curve
Phillips curve
Demand curve
Aggregate supply curve
context: Normally upward-sloping (longer maturities pay more to compensate for term risk). Inversions, where short maturities pay more, often signal coming recession via Fed tightening expectations.

question: When you buy a share of stock, you become:
answer: A fractional owner of the corporation
choices: A fractional owner of the corporation
A lender to the corporation
A bondholder of the corporation
A customer of the corporation
context: Plus voting rights, residual claims on earnings (dividends), and residual claim in liquidation (after debt). Different share classes get different rights.

question: The Nasdaq Composite Index reached its dot-com bubble peak in:
answer: March 2000 at 5048
choices: March 2000 at 5048
January 2000 at 4000
December 1999 at 5000
October 1999 at 3000
context: Fell to 1114 by October 2002 — a 78% peak-to-trough decline. Many high-profile firms went bankrupt; valuations had massively exceeded any plausible discounted cash flow.

question: Vote-trading among legislators — 'support my pork and I'll support yours' — is called:
answer: Logrolling
choices: Logrolling
Riding piggyback
Capture
Rent-seeking
context: Buchanan and Tullock formalized the analysis in The Calculus of Consent. Concentrated benefits + dispersed costs + log-rolling = the textbook recipe for swollen, wasteful public spending.

question: Hernando de Soto's 2000 book argued that the world's poor are locked out of capitalism because they lack:
answer: Formal property records they can borrow against.
choices: Formal property records they can borrow against.
Modern technology
Trade access to global markets
Subsidies from rich countries
context: Estimated $9 trillion of 'dead capital' worldwide. Formalize property titles and the poor can use their assets as collateral. A Hayekian institutional reform agenda.

question: David Landes's 1998 work on why some nations grew rich while others did not was titled:
answer: The Wealth and Poverty of Nations
choices: The Wealth and Poverty of Nations
Why Nations Fail
The Mystery of Capital
The Rise of the West
context: Magisterial. Argued culture, climate, and geography all matter, alongside institutions. Often criticized by political-economists who prefer pure institutional explanations.

question: Warren Buffett famously bet against hedge funds over a 10-year period from 2008 to 2017. The result:
answer: Buffett's index fund handily outperformed
choices: Buffett's index fund handily outperformed
Hedge funds won by a wide margin.
It was a near tie.
The bet was called off.
context: Buffett's S&P 500 index returned 7.1% annually; hedge funds returned 2.2%. The $1M proceeds went to Girls Inc. of Omaha. A vivid lesson in passive investing.

question: Tesla announced a $1.5B Bitcoin purchase in February 2021, then later sold roughly what fraction in mid-2022?
answer: About 75% of the holding
choices: About 75% of the holding
All of it
None — Tesla still holds it all
context: Elon Musk cited liquidity needs during a difficult quarter. Tesla still holds some Bitcoin. The episode showed how corporate Bitcoin treasury decisions face short-term pressures.

question: Hong Kong has maintained an unusual currency-board regime tying its dollar to the US dollar since:
context: The Linked Exchange Rate System. Hong Kong's monetary base is fully backed by USD reserves at a fixed rate. A working example of currency-board discipline; long the world's freest economy.

question: The Czech Republic, like Poland, kept its own currency rather than adopt the euro. The Czech currency is the:
answer: Koruna
choices: Koruna
Zloty
Forint
Tolar
context: The Czech National Bank has run a more conservative monetary policy than the ECB. The economy has prospered with this independence. The euro debate continues but adoption is not imminent.

question: By November 15, 1923, one US dollar bought how many German marks at the worst of Weimar hyperinflation?
answer: About 4.2 trillion marks
choices: About 4.2 trillion marks
About 100,000 marks
About 1 billion marks
About 100 marks
context: From 4.2 marks per dollar in 1914. A nine-year debasement of nearly 12 orders of magnitude. The Rentenmark stabilization was treated as an economic miracle.

question: The First Bank of the United States's 20-year charter expired without renewal in:
context: The vote to renew failed by one in each chamber of Congress. The country went through the War of 1812 with no central bank — a chaotic monetary experience that pushed renewal.

question: The National Banking Acts of 1863-64 effectively ended state bank note issuance by:
answer: Imposing a 10% federal tax on state-bank notes
choices: Imposing a 10% federal tax on state-bank notes
Outlawing state bank charters
Confiscating state-bank reserves
Federalizing all state banks
context: Tax made state bank notes uncirculable. National bank notes — secured by Treasury bonds — replaced them. A subtle but devastating use of taxing power to consolidate monetary issuance.

question: After helping design the Federal Reserve at Jekyll Island, Paul Warburg served on the Fed's:
answer: First Federal Reserve Board (1914-1918)
choices: First Federal Reserve Board (1914-1918)
First New York Fed presidency
First FOMC
Federal Advisory Council
context: Resigned amid wartime anti-German pressure. His brother Max Warburg ran a German private bank. A reminder of how international the founding generation of central bankers was.

question: The Bank of Japan from 2016 explicitly pegged the 10-year JGB yield near zero, an experiment called:
answer: Yield Curve Control (YCC)
choices: Yield Curve Control (YCC)
Quantitative Easing
Operation Twist
Zero Lower Bound policy
context: By committing to buy unlimited JGBs at the target yield, the BoJ effectively pegged the long end of the curve. The policy slowly unwound through 2024 as inflation forced reconsideration.

question: Adam Smith's hometown — and the seaside Scottish village where he wrote much of Wealth of Nations — was:
answer: Kirkcaldy
choices: Kirkcaldy
Edinburgh
Glasgow
Dunfermline
context: Across the Firth of Forth from Edinburgh. Smith returned to live with his mother during the writing. The book took ten years to complete. Kirkcaldy maintains a small Smith museum.

question: Adam Smith's closest friend, who died in 1776 just before Wealth of Nations was published, was the Scottish philosopher:
answer: David Hume
choices: David Hume
Frances Hutcheson
Adam Ferguson
Thomas Reid
context: Smith wrote a remarkable account of Hume's serene atheist deathbed. The piece scandalized religious readers; Smith remarked it caused him 'ten times more abuse' than Wealth of Nations would.

question: David Card's 1990 study of the Mariel boatlift, in which 125,000 Cubans suddenly arrived in Miami, found:
answer: Little measurable impact on native wages
choices: Little measurable impact on native wages
Severe wage suppression for natives
Substantial unemployment increases
Major price inflation
context: Used as evidence in immigration policy debates. George Borjas later disputed Card's findings. The empirical questions are genuinely complex; the policy debate continues.

question: North and Weingast's 1989 paper showed England's post-1689 economic takeoff came from:
answer: Constraining the crown's taxing and borrowing
choices: Constraining the crown's taxing and borrowing
Expanding democratic representation
The Bank of England's founding
The East India Company's growth
context: Credible commitment to honor debts and property opened access to capital markets. Property rights as a complex bundle of credible institutions, not just legal forms.

question: In 1871 a 31-year-old Austrian journalist named Carl Menger published a slim volume overturning classical value theory. Where, he argued, does value come from?
answer: From subjective valuations of individuals making choices
choices: From subjective valuations of individuals making choices
From the average labor hours required for production
From equilibrium of aggregate supply and demand curves
From the historical cost of capital invested in the good
context: Menger's Grundsatze launched the Austrian school. The classicals were stuck on labor and cost; Menger showed value lives in the human mind ranking ends.

question: Mises's praxeology rests on a starting proposition he called the action axiom. The axiom is so basic that denying it is self-refuting. What does it state?
answer: Humans act purposefully, using means to attain ends
choices: Humans act purposefully, using means to attain ends
All value is created by socially necessary labor.
Markets always clear at the equilibrium price
Aggregate demand drives the level of activity
context: Try to deny it and you have acted: you have purposefully chosen the end of denying it. Mises built deductive economics on this rock.

question: In 1931-32 a public debate erupted between Hayek at LSE and Keynes at Cambridge. The argument centered on Keynes's 1930 book. Which book?
answer: A Treatise on Money — Keynes's pre-General-Theory work
choices: A Treatise on Money — Keynes's pre-General-Theory work
The General Theory — Keynes's 1936 macro masterwork
Economic Consequences of the Peace — his 1919 critique
How to Pay for the War — his 1940 wartime pamphlet
context: Hayek's review of the Treatise was savage and technical. Keynes counterpunched but then abandoned the field, writing the General Theory instead.

question: In September 1945 Hayek published a short essay in the American Economic Review naming what no central planner could have. What did he name it?
answer: The knowledge problem — dispersed, local, tacit information
choices: The knowledge problem — dispersed, local, tacit information
The calculation problem — impossibility of socialist prices
The information asymmetry problem — buyers and sellers
The principal-agent problem — managers versus owners
context: Hayek's The Use of Knowledge in Society. The relevant knowledge sits in the heads of every farmer and trader; prices coordinate it. No Moscow bureau can replicate it.

question: Thomas Sowell's 2000 book taught core economic principles to readers without math or jargon. It has gone through multiple editions and sold over a million copies. What is its title?
answer: Basic Economics — a citizen's guide to the economy
choices: Basic Economics — a citizen's guide to the economy
Knowledge and Decisions — his 1980 Hayekian treatise
Marxism: Philosophy and Economics — his 1985 critique
Intellectuals and Society — his 2009 critique of elites
context: Basic Economics explains price signals, rent control, minimum wages, and trade in clear English a high-schooler grasps. Sowell's gift to the public.

question: In 1980 Milton Friedman hosted a 10-part PBS series and companion book promoting free-market ideas to a mass audience. What was it called?
answer: Free to Choose — co-written with his wife Rose Director
choices: Free to Choose — co-written with his wife Rose Director
Capitalism and Freedom — based on his earlier 1962 book
Money Mischief — based on his later 1992 monetary history
The Tyranny of the Status Quo — his 1984 political book
context: Free to Choose aired during the Reagan campaign and shaped public opinion. Episodes covered welfare, schools, regulation, and inflation — Milton in his 60s at peak influence.

question: In 1937 a 27-year-old Ronald Coase published a famously short essay asking: if markets are so efficient, why do firms exist at all? His answer named what economic concept?
answer: Transaction costs — friction of negotiating and enforcing
choices: Transaction costs — friction of negotiating and enforcing
Returns to scale — large firms produce more cheaply
Market failure — externalities need central coordination
Comparative advantage — firms specialize in their strength
context: Firms exist because using the market has costs: searching, negotiating, enforcing. Internalize transactions until cost of one more in-house equals one more contract. Coase was 27.

question: In 1850 the Frenchman Frederic Bastiat published his last essay, a parable about a baker's broken window. What distinction did it introduce?
answer: Between what is seen and what is not seen — visible vs forgone.
choices: Between what is seen and what is not seen — visible vs forgone.
Between the short run and the long run in economic adjustment
Between nominal value and real value adjusted for inflation
Between average cost and marginal cost in production decisions
context: What is seen: the glazier paid to fix the window. What is unseen: everything else the baker would have spent that money on. The fallacy lives on every time someone claims a hurricane stimulates the economy.

question: Nassim Taleb's 2007 book argued that rare, high-impact, unpredictable events shape history more than bell-curve thinking. What did he call such events?
answer: Black swans — extreme outliers prevailing models cannot foresee
choices: Black swans — extreme outliers prevailing models cannot foresee
Gray rhinos — obvious dangers ignored until they charge
White elephants — costly assets that yield little value
Red tape — bureaucratic obstacles slowing productive activity
context: Taleb published The Black Swan a year before Lehman collapsed. The 2008 crisis was a fat-tail event Gaussian risk models had assigned near-zero probability. Taleb was vindicated.

question: In 2012 Nassim Taleb coined a new word naming a property he argued was crucial — and that fragile institutions lacked. What was the word?
answer: Antifragile — systems that gain from disorder and stress
choices: Antifragile — systems that gain from disorder and stress
Counterfragile — systems that resist disorder without breaking
Hyperfragile — systems that fail catastrophically under stress
Crystallographic — systems with hidden structural weak points
context: Robust resists disorder; antifragile thrives on it. Muscles grow under stress, immune systems via challenge, markets via volatility. Bailouts make banking fragile by removing the stress that keeps it honest.

question: Murray Rothbard wrote a short 1962 pamphlet making the case for restoring sound money. The question-titled cover is iconic in Austrian circles. What is its title?
answer: What Has Government Done to Our Money?
choices: What Has Government Done to Our Money?
Why Is Inflation So Hard to Stop?
Where Did All the Gold Go?
How Did the Federal Reserve Begin?
context: Rothbard's 1962 pamphlet remains the cleanest introduction to sound money. He traces money from market emergence through state debasement, central banking, and fiat — all in 100 pages.

question: Walter Block's 1976 book provoked outrage by defending the rights — under a libertarian framework — of people most readers would consider villains. What was the title?
answer: Defending the Undefendable — the pimp, the prostitute, the moneylender
choices: Defending the Undefendable — the pimp, the prostitute, the moneylender
The Anti-Capitalist Mentality — Mises's 1956 attack on intellectuals
The Politics of Obedience — La Boetie on voluntary servitude
Liberty Defined — Ron Paul's 2011 collection of essays
context: Block argued non-aggressive but disreputable actors — usurers, scalpers, slumlords — were misunderstood. Hayek wrote: 'Looking through it has been a good cure of any leftish remnants.' Vintage Block.

question: Austrian Business Cycle Theory also explains the late-1990s tech bubble. What Fed-era setup created the malinvestment boom that ended in March 2000?
answer: Easy credit and persistent rate cuts through the late 1990s
choices: Easy credit and persistent rate cuts through the late 1990s
Tariffs on imported semiconductors raised by NAFTA disputes
Y2K legislation forcing tech rebuilds at government expense
Capital-gains tax cuts that channeled all savings into stocks
context: Greenspan's accommodative policy fueled tech speculation. Nasdaq peaked March 10, 2000 at 5,048; by October 2002 it had lost 78%. ABCT names the cycle; the Fed runs it.

question: Adam Smith wrote a major work BEFORE The Wealth of Nations, in 1759, on moral psychology and the social emotions. What is its title?
answer: The Theory of Moral Sentiments — sympathy and moral judgment
choices: The Theory of Moral Sentiments — sympathy and moral judgment
The Lectures on Jurisprudence — published posthumously
The Philosophy of Natural Law — never finished or published
The Origins of Money — his thesis on monetary emergence
context: Smith was a moral philosopher first. Moral Sentiments grounds Wealth of Nations: market exchange works because we have sympathy and judge each other's conduct. The two books were one project.

question: Karl Marx predicted in Capital (1867) that capitalism would self-destruct through a specific tendency in the profit rate over time. What did he predict?
answer: A secular fall in the rate of profit driving capitalism to crisis
choices: A secular fall in the rate of profit driving capitalism to crisis
A secular rise in the rate of profit concentrating wealth
A stable rate of profit with declining wages over time
A volatile rate of profit with sharper short-run cycles
context: Marx's prediction failed. Bohm-Bawerk demolished the underlying labor theory in 1896. The actual long-run record of capitalist economies: rising wages, rising productivity, rising standards of living — opposite of Marx.

question: Lew Rockwell founded the Ludwig von Mises Institute in 1982. He had previously served as chief of staff to a young Texas congressman who shared his hard-money politics. Whose chief of staff?
answer: Ron Paul — Texas Republican, Austrian-school sympathizer
choices: Ron Paul — Texas Republican, Austrian-school sympathizer
Phil Gramm — Texas Republican, deregulation senator
Newt Gingrich — Georgia Republican, later House Speaker
Dick Armey — Texas Republican, Contract with America
context: Rockwell's tenure with Paul (1978-82) put him at the intersection of Austrian economics and elected politics. The Mises Institute followed — combining serious scholarship with a popular reach that academic Austrian programs lacked.

question: W.H. Hutt, a 20th-century South African economist of the LSE tradition, wrote a forceful classical-liberal critique of organized labor and the General Theory. What was his most cited later book?
answer: The Strike-Threat System — coercive labor power critique
choices: The Strike-Threat System — coercive labor power critique
The Theory of Idle Resources — his 1939 Keynes rebuttal
Politically Impossible — his 1971 democratic-process critique
The Keynesian Episode — his 1979 retrospective on Keynes
context: Hutt's career spanned the Mises-Hayek period through the 1980s. His Theory of Idle Resources demolished Keynes's involuntary-unemployment claim. The Strike-Threat System (1973) is still cited in labor-economics debate.

question: Carl Menger's son Karl Menger Jr. became a famous mathematician and a member of the Vienna Circle. What was his mathematical specialty?
answer: General topology and dimension theory
choices: General topology and dimension theory
Linear algebra and matrix decomposition
Differential geometry and Riemannian manifolds
Number theory and algebraic structures
context: Karl Menger Jr. (1902-1985) was a mathematician of distinction in his own right — Menger sponge, Menger curvature. He preserved his father's papers and helped bring the Austrian legacy to America.

question: Friedrich Hayek arrived at the London School of Economics in early 1931 to deliver the Tooke Lectures that would launch his English career. Who arranged the invitation?
answer: Lionel Robbins, then heading the LSE economics department
choices: Lionel Robbins, then heading the LSE economics department
John Maynard Keynes from rival Cambridge — generous to a foe
William Beveridge, the LSE director and welfare-state architect
Friedrich Engels's grandson Alfred Marshall's heir
context: Robbins read Hayek's work on monetary theory and saw a serious challenger to Keynes. The four Tooke Lectures became Prices and Production. Hayek stayed at LSE until 1950, joining Chicago at war's end of intellectual fashion.

question: Ludwig von Mises's unpaid NYU appointment (1945-69) needed an outside funding source for his actual salary. Who was the principal patron?
answer: Lawrence Fertig — businessman, New York World-Telegram columnist
choices: Lawrence Fertig — businessman, New York World-Telegram columnist
Henry Ford — Detroit industrialist, anti-Roosevelt politician
John D. Rockefeller Jr. — Standard Oil heir
Andrew Carnegie — steel magnate, libertarian philanthropist
context: Fertig and the William Volker Charities Fund quietly underwrote Mises's American career. Without them, the most important economist of his generation might have ended his life in unfunded obscurity.

question: Karl Popper's philosophy of science centered on a single criterion distinguishing science from non-science. What is the criterion?
answer: Falsifiability — a theory must specify what would refute it.
choices: Falsifiability — a theory must specify what would refute it.
Verifiability — a theory must be confirmable by observation.
Coherence — a theory must be internally logically consistent.
Simplicity — a theory must be the parsimonious account.
context: Popper: Marxism and psychoanalysis explain everything and predict nothing specific that could refute them — non-science. Einstein's general relativity predicted a precise observation that could have falsified it — science. Influenced Hayek, von Mises responded with praxeology.

question: George Akerlof's 1970 paper analyzed how information asymmetry between buyers and sellers can cause markets to break down. What example did he use?
answer: The used-car market — sellers know quality, buyers don't
choices: The used-car market — sellers know quality, buyers don't
The insurance market — insureds know risk, insurers don't
The labor market — workers know ability, employers don't
The lending market — borrowers know risk, lenders don't
context: The Market for 'Lemons' won Akerlof the 2001 Nobel and launched information economics. Note: it modeled a market failure but is often misread — Austrians point out that warranties, dealerships, and Carfax all solve the problem.

question: Russ Roberts, a Stanford Hoover scholar and former GMU professor, has hosted a long-running interview podcast on economics since 2006. What is the podcast?
answer: EconTalk — weekly hour-long conversations on economics
choices: EconTalk — weekly hour-long conversations on economics
Capital Ideas — Hoover-published policy interviews
Free Thoughts — Cato-published libertarian discussions
Knowledge@Wharton — business school faculty interviews
context: EconTalk has interviewed every major free-market economist alive plus many non-economists on economic topics. Roberts's gentle questioning style has made the podcast the gold standard of long-form economics conversation.

question: Carl Menger's 1871 founding work was titled in German Grundsatze der Volkswirtschaftslehre. What did the title translate to in English?
answer: Principles of Economics
choices: Principles of Economics
Foundations of Political Economy
Elements of Subjective Value Theory
Lectures on Economic Theory
context: The English translation appeared only in 1950, decades after the original. James Dingwall and Bert Hoselitz translated. Menger's German prose is dense; the wait until English speakers could read him slowed Austrian school spread.

question: Friedrich Hayek died at age 92 in Germany, having lived to see Berlin Wall fall and Soviet planning collapse — vindicating his lifetime's argument. In what year did he die?
answer: 1992 — three years after the Berlin Wall came down.
choices: 1992 — three years after the Berlin Wall came down.
1986 — three years before the Soviet collapse
1995 — at the height of the post-Cold-War liberal moment
1980 — before Reagan's election as US president
context: Hayek died March 23, 1992. The Velvet Revolution, the Berlin Wall, and Yeltsin's standing on the Russian tank had all happened. The Fatal Conceit had been published 1988. He died vindicated by history.

question: When the Nazis swept into France in 1940, Mises and his wife Margit fled across Spain and Portugal to reach New York. He arrived as a 59-year-old refugee with no academic position. From what city did he depart Europe?
answer: Lisbon — final European port before the Atlantic crossing
choices: Lisbon — final European port before the Atlantic crossing
Madrid — overland route through Spain to Mediterranean ports
Genoa — Italian ports more open than Iberian ones for refugees
Marseille — French south coast still officially neutral
context: The Lisbon route saved thousands of Jewish refugees. Mises took six weeks getting from Geneva to Lisbon to New York. His Vienna library had to be abandoned; he later got most of it back.

question: Eugen von Bohm-Bawerk served three times as Austrian finance minister in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. He resigned each time over the same issue. What issue?
answer: Refusing to sanction increased deficit spending and currency debasement
choices: Refusing to sanction increased deficit spending and currency debasement
Conflict with the imperial court over Bohemian tariff arrangements
Disagreement over imperial railroad pricing and labor regulations
Disputes over colonial expansion into Balkan and Adriatic markets
context: Bohm-Bawerk insisted on sound money and balanced budgets when these were unfashionable. His resignations preserved his intellectual integrity but limited his political influence. Austrian fiscal discipline was lost after his retirement; debasement followed.

question: In March 1993 Eric Hughes published a short founding document for the cypherpunk movement. Its opening line is famous: 'Privacy is necessary for an open society in the electronic age.' What was the title?
answer: A Cypherpunk's Manifesto — Eric Hughes, 1993
choices: A Cypherpunk's Manifesto — Eric Hughes, 1993
Crypto Anarchy Manifesto — Tim May, 1988.
A Declaration of Cyberspace Independence — John Perry Barlow, 1996
The Code Book — Simon Singh, 1999
context: Hughes wrote 'Cypherpunks write code.' The manifesto distilled the movement's ethos: privacy is fundamental, software is power, no permission needed. Bitcoin's anonymity, transparency, and permissionless openness all flow from this lineage.

question: In 1991 Phil Zimmermann released a free email-encryption program that for the first time put strong public-key cryptography in the hands of ordinary users. What was it called?
answer: PGP — Pretty Good Privacy, free public-key encryption
choices: PGP — Pretty Good Privacy, free public-key encryption
TLS — Transport Layer Security, web encryption
S/MIME — Secure Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions
RSA — the underlying public-key algorithm itself
context: Zimmermann faced US federal investigation for exporting munitions (PGP) by posting source code online. The case fell apart by 1996. PGP became the standard email-encryption tool and proved that cryptography was uncontrollable speech.

question: Bitcoin miners compete to find a specific kind of number that, when hashed together with the rest of a block, produces an output below a target threshold. What is this number called?
answer: Nonce — a number-once-used in block headers, varied until target met
choices: Nonce — a number-once-used in block headers, varied until target met
Seed — the initial randomness for block creation
Salt — additional randomness mixed into the password hashing
Hash — the output of the hashing function, not the input
context: Miners adjust the nonce trillions of times per second, hashing the block header until the output starts with enough leading zeros to meet the difficulty target. Whoever finds it first broadcasts the block and earns the reward.

question: A widely-shared phrase summarizing the lesson of Mt. Gox, FTX, and many other exchange collapses warns Bitcoin holders against trusting third parties with their coins. What is the phrase?
answer: Not your keys, not your coins
choices: Not your keys, not your coins
Not your wallet, not your money
Not your seed, not your stack
Not your address, not your asset
context: Andreas Antonopoulos popularized the phrase. Custody risk is real and recurring: Mt. Gox 2014, QuadrigaCX 2018, Celsius 2022, FTX 2022. Self-custody hardware wallets eliminate the counterparty risk entirely — that's the point.

question: As Bitcoin's block subsidy halves toward zero, miner revenue must increasingly come from another source. What source?
answer: Transaction fees paid by users for inclusion in blocks
choices: Transaction fees paid by users for inclusion in blocks
Government subsidies to ensure continued mining operations
A new emission mechanism added by future protocol upgrade
Direct payments from large holders to maintain network security
context: The economics of Bitcoin's long-term security depends on transaction fees becoming sufficient. Some argue fee markets won't sustain enough security; others argue layer 2 settlement traffic will. Decades remain to find out which is right.

question: A specific Bitcoin wallet feature allows you to share a single string with merchants or accountants that lets them see all incoming transactions to your wallet, without giving them the power to spend. What is this string called?
answer: Extended public key (xpub) — view-only wallet access
choices: Extended public key (xpub) — view-only wallet access
Private key — would allow spending, not just viewing.
Public key hash — only enables one address, not the whole wallet
Mnemonic phrase — gives full control, not view-only
context: An xpub derives all your receive addresses but cannot sign transactions. Useful for accountants, payment processors, or family monitoring. Caution: an xpub reveals your wallet's entire transaction history — privacy implications.

question: Nick Szabo coined a phrase about a specific property valuable goods historically share — they cost something real to produce or acquire. What did he call this property?
answer: Unforgeable costliness — verifiable real-resource cost to produce
choices: Unforgeable costliness — verifiable real-resource cost to produce
Visible scarcity — easily observable supply limits
Cultural recognition — historical use as a store of value
Industrial utility — non-monetary practical applications
context: Gold requires mining; Bitcoin requires hash power. Both are unforgeably costly. Fiat currency is not. Szabo's framing is one bridge from Austrian monetary theory to Bitcoin: hard money requires physical work to create.

question: After the DAO hack, the Ethereum community faced a choice: accept the loss or revert it via a protocol change. What did they decide?
answer: They hard-forked to reverse the hack and refund DAO investors
choices: They hard-forked to reverse the hack and refund DAO investors
They accepted the loss as a learning experience about smart contracts
They froze the funds permanently in a multi-signature contract
They negotiated a payment from the hacker to release the funds
context: Ethereum's July 2016 hard fork erased the hacker's gains. Dissenters refused and continued mining the original chain as Ethereum Classic (ETC). This single event shows Ethereum is not credibly neutral — the rules can be changed for sufficient cause.

question: Tether, the largest stablecoin by market cap, has faced repeated questions about whether its USDT tokens are fully backed by US dollar reserves. What was the central concern over the years?
answer: Whether USDT was truly 1:1 backed by audited dollar reserves.
choices: Whether USDT was truly 1:1 backed by audited dollar reserves.
Whether USDT could be redeemed at all under any circumstances.
Whether USDT was technically inflated by miner pre-mines.
Whether USDT had a Ponzi-scheme distribution structure.
context: Tether settled with NYAG in 2021 for $18.5M after admitting reserves had not always been 1:1 backed. Reserves now reportedly include short-term Treasury bills and other instruments. The opacity persists; the systemic risk persists.

question: Sam Bankman-Fried's trial concluded in October 2023 with conviction on all charges. How many counts did the jury convict him of?
answer: Seven counts including wire fraud, securities fraud, and money laundering
choices: Seven counts including wire fraud, securities fraud, and money laundering
Three counts of various securities violations only
Twelve counts including racketeering and tax evasion
Two counts of wire fraud, with the rest dropped pre-trial
context: The jury deliberated only a few hours before unanimous conviction on all seven counts. SBF testified in his own defense disastrously. His sentence of 25 years matches his prosecutor Damian Williams's request closely. EA-funded political laundering schemes did not save him.

question: FTX's affiliated trading firm was run by Sam Bankman-Fried's deputy, who pleaded guilty and cooperated with prosecutors before SBF's trial. What was her name?
answer: Caroline Ellison — Alameda CEO who pleaded guilty
choices: Caroline Ellison — Alameda CEO who pleaded guilty
Gary Wang — FTX cofounder who also pleaded guilty
Nishad Singh — FTX engineer who also pleaded guilty
Ryan Salame — FTX executive who pleaded guilty separately
context: Ellison's testimony helped convict SBF. She received a 2-year sentence. The MIT-pedigreed Effective Altruism connections of the FTX inner circle became a cultural touchstone for crypto skepticism — the smartest people in the room committed massive fraud.

question: Terra/Luna's founder fled after the collapse and was apprehended in March 2023. Where?
answer: Montenegro, while trying to fly out on a forged passport
choices: Montenegro, while trying to fly out on a forged passport
Singapore, where Terra was headquartered formally.
South Korea, where he had returned to face charges.
Dubai, where he had been residing for cover.
context: Kwon was arrested at Podgorica airport, then extradited and faces both US and South Korean charges. The Terra collapse erased estimated investor losses of $40 billion+. Crypto's algorithmic-stablecoin moment ended in disaster.

question: In December 2018 a Canadian crypto exchange's CEO died suddenly in India, allegedly taking control of customer funds (~$190M) to his grave. What was the exchange?
answer: QuadrigaCX — Gerald Cotten died in India in December 2018.
choices: QuadrigaCX — Gerald Cotten died in India in December 2018.
Mt. Gox — Mark Karpeles arrested but never died.
Mt Pelerin — separate Swiss exchange not affected
Cryptopia — New Zealand exchange hacked separately in 2019
context: Subsequent investigations suggest Cotten had been running QuadrigaCX as a Ponzi long before his death. Whether he is actually dead remains disputed. Customers lost most of their funds; the case is now studied as fraud, not just custody failure.

question: In 2017 a wave of Initial Coin Offerings raised billions from retail investors. The vast majority produced little or nothing. What proportion of 2017 ICOs failed?
answer: Estimated over 80% failed, were abandoned, or were fraudulent.
choices: Estimated over 80% failed, were abandoned, or were fraudulent.
Estimated under 10% failed — most projects succeeded
Estimated around 50% — split between success and failure
Estimated under 20% — most merged into larger ecosystems
context: Studies put the failure rate at 78-92%. The SEC began enforcement in 2018, classifying most ICOs as unregistered securities. The era left a generation of retail investors burned and skeptical of 'utility tokens.'

question: Most Bitcoin mining occurs through specific economic arrangements where miners combine their hash power for steady payouts. What are these called?
answer: Mining pools — Foundry, AntPool, F2Pool, ViaBTC, etc.
choices: Mining pools — Foundry, AntPool, F2Pool, ViaBTC, etc.
Mining cartels — illegal collusion among miners
Mining cooperatives — non-profit miner-owned associations
Mining trusts — financial vehicles holding mining rewards
context: Pool concentration is a known concern: a handful of pools control most hashrate. Stratum V2 aims to mitigate by returning template choice to individual miners. Bitcoin's resilience to pool centralization is an ongoing topic of governance.

question: Many Bitcoin users run their nodes through a privacy-preserving network that hides their IP address from peers. What is this network?
answer: Tor — onion routing for IP-address anonymity
choices: Tor — onion routing for IP-address anonymity
VPN — virtual private network for IP masking
I2P — invisible Internet project, smaller alternative to Tor
Mixnet — generic privacy-preserving network architecture
context: Tor support has been in Bitcoin Core for years. Running over Tor masks the connection between your IP address and your transactions — critical for serious self-custody privacy. Antonopoulos has long advocated this practice.

question: Bitcoin's white paper is famously short. How many pages does it span?
answer: Nine pages including references — concise by design
choices: Nine pages including references — concise by design
Forty-eight pages including detailed appendices
Three pages — too short for the actual technical content
Twenty-five pages with extensive mathematical proofs
context: Satoshi's white paper is nine pages — section by section: introduction, transactions, timestamp server, proof-of-work, network, incentive, reclaiming disk space, simplified payment verification, combining and splitting value, privacy, calculations. Tight, clear, complete.

question: A famous Bitcoin community phrase originated as a drunken typo on a forum post in 2013 and became iconic shorthand for long-term holding. What is the phrase?
answer: HODL — originated December 18, 2013 BitcoinTalk post by 'GameKyuubi'
choices: HODL — originated December 18, 2013 BitcoinTalk post by 'GameKyuubi'
BTFD — buy the dip, generic crypto-trader vocabulary
MOON — generic crypto-speculator slogan, not specific origin
WAGMI — we're all going to make it, more recent NFT vocabulary
context: The original post 'I AM HODLING' was typed during a steep BTC price drop by an admittedly drunk user. The community adopted it as 'Hold On for Dear Life.' HODL captures Bitcoin's core thesis: time horizons matter more than timing.

question: Around 600 BC a Mediterranean kingdom became the first place in history to mint standardized coins, transforming commerce. Which kingdom?
answer: Lydia, in western Anatolia, under King Alyattes or his son Croesus
choices: Lydia, in western Anatolia, under King Alyattes or his son Croesus
Persia, under Cyrus the Great, who later adopted Lydian methods
Egypt, under the Late Period pharaohs of the 26th Dynasty
Sparta, under the laws of Lycurgus the legendary lawgiver
context: Lydian coins of electrum (gold-silver alloy) were the world's first state-backed coined money. King Croesus's wealth became proverbial. The innovation spread to Greek city-states and changed Mediterranean commerce permanently.

question: The Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire minted a gold coin that held its weight and purity for an unprecedented duration. What was the coin called and how long did it hold?
answer: Solidus — held its standard weight and purity for over 700 years.
choices: Solidus — held its standard weight and purity for over 700 years.
Denarius — held its standard for 700 years before debasement.
Drachma — held its standard for 1,000 years through the medieval era.
Dinar — held its standard for 500 years across the Islamic world.
context: The solidus (later bezant in trade) was the gold standard of medieval trade from Constantinople to China. Stable money attracted commerce; commerce funded Byzantium's resilience. A model of monetary discipline rare in history.

question: Spain's silver coin became the world's first global currency, circulating from Mexico to Manila to Manchuria. What was it called?
answer: Pieces of Eight — the Spanish silver dollar, eight reales
choices: Pieces of Eight — the Spanish silver dollar, eight reales
Doubloons — Spanish gold coins, separate from the pieces of eight
Maravedis — Spanish copper coins of much smaller value
Real de a ocho — same coin, also known as Spanish dollar
context: The Spanish dollar dominated global commerce for centuries. American colonists called them dollars; the US dollar inherited the name. The peso, the yuan, and many other currencies trace lineage to this Spanish coin.

question: In the Dutch Republic of the 1630s, a speculative bubble in flower bulbs reached extraordinary peaks before collapsing in 1637. What flower was involved?
answer: Tulip — Dutch tulip mania, the first recorded speculative bubble
choices: Tulip — Dutch tulip mania, the first recorded speculative bubble
Carnation — separate later speculative episode in Spain
Daffodil — never the subject of a major bubble
Rose — never the subject of a major bubble
context: Single tulip bulbs reportedly traded for the price of a townhouse in Amsterdam. The collapse came in February 1637. The episode is the standard reference for asset-bubble psychology — though revisionist historians argue the scale has been exaggerated.

question: In 1720 England suffered its own great financial bubble in parallel with France's, centered on a joint-stock company. What was the company called?
answer: The South Sea Company — granted monopoly on trade with Spanish America
choices: The South Sea Company — granted monopoly on trade with Spanish America
The East India Company — much older and more successful entity
The Royal African Company — slave-trading monopoly, separate bubble
The Hudson's Bay Company — Canadian fur-trading concern
context: South Sea Company shares rose tenfold in 1720 on inflated trade prospects, then collapsed. Newton lost a fortune; Walpole used the crisis to consolidate his power. Parliament passed the Bubble Act restricting joint-stock companies for over a century.

question: Under the Classical Gold Standard, one nation's currency served as the de facto world reserve money. Which one?
answer: Pound sterling, anchored to gold by Britain since 1717
choices: Pound sterling, anchored to gold by Britain since 1717
French franc, used widely across European colonial empires
German mark, only after the unified empire formed in 1871
Russian ruble, in eastern European and central Asian trade
context: Newton (as Master of the Mint, 1699-1727) had fixed the pound to gold at a rate that became durable. The Bank of England's discipline and London's capital markets gave sterling pre-1914 the role the US dollar would assume post-1944.

question: At Bretton Woods two negotiators stood opposed over the basic structure of the postwar monetary system. Who were they?
answer: John Maynard Keynes for Britain, Harry Dexter White for the United States
choices: John Maynard Keynes for Britain, Harry Dexter White for the United States
Lord Beveridge for Britain, Herbert Hoover for the United States
Walter Lippmann for the US, Paul Ramadier for France
Maynard Keynes for Britain, Andre Tardieu for France
context: Keynes wanted a global Bancor currency administered by a true international institution. White wanted the US dollar at the system's center. The US held the gold and won the argument. White was later identified as a Soviet asset by Venona transcripts.

question: In August 1971 a US president unilaterally ended the Bretton Woods system on national television. Who, and what did he do?
answer: Richard Nixon — closed the gold window, ending dollar convertibility
choices: Richard Nixon — closed the gold window, ending dollar convertibility
Lyndon Johnson — devalued the dollar by 10% against gold
John F. Kennedy — restricted gold sales to foreign central banks
Gerald Ford — abandoned the IMF's parity rate system permanently
context: Nixon's televised announcement on August 15, 1971 'temporarily' suspended gold convertibility. The temporary closure became permanent. The world entered the fiat era — currencies floating against each other, anchored to nothing.

question: After Bretton Woods collapsed, gold's price rose dramatically against the inflating dollar. What level did gold reach in January 1980?
answer: Approximately $850 per ounce at the peak in January 1980
choices: Approximately $850 per ounce at the peak in January 1980
Approximately $100 per ounce at the peak in January 1980
Approximately $2,000 per ounce at the peak in January 1980
Approximately $400 per ounce at the peak in January 1980
context: Gold's price had been $35/oz under Bretton Woods. By 1980 inflation was 14%, oil was in crisis, and gold surged to $850. The Hunt brothers' silver corner peaked the same month. Volcker's high rates broke the inflation; gold then fell hard.

question: The Coinage Act of 1873 demonetized silver in the United States, transitioning to a pure gold standard. Silver advocates later denounced this as something specific. What did they call it?
answer: The Crime of '73 — silver demonetization by stealth
choices: The Crime of '73 — silver demonetization by stealth
The Great Demonetization — formal title in silver-advocacy literature
The Bimetallic Betrayal — informal label rarely used historically
The Hard Money Coup — academic later description
context: Silver miners and inflation-leaning farmers viewed the 1873 act as a banker's conspiracy. The 'Crime of '73' framing fueled the Free Silver movement that produced Bryan's 1896 cross-of-gold speech. Sound-money historians dispute the conspiracy framing.

question: In 1900 Congress formally defined the dollar in terms of a specific weight of gold, ending decades of bimetallic dispute. What did the act establish?
answer: The dollar at 25.8 grains of gold 9/10 fine — a gold standard until 1933
choices: The dollar at 25.8 grains of gold 9/10 fine — a gold standard until 1933
A complete bimetallic standard with both gold and silver
A floating exchange rate against European currencies
Free silver coinage at a ratio of 16-to-1 with gold
context: The Gold Standard Act of 1900 was the high tide of formal US gold-standard monetary policy. It would last 33 years until FDR's confiscation. The American era of stable money — and remarkable economic growth — was real.

question: The worst hyperinflation in recorded history occurred in a single Central European country in 1946. Which country, and how fast did prices double at the peak?
answer: Hungary — prices doubled every 15 hours at the 1946 peak
choices: Hungary — prices doubled every 15 hours at the 1946 peak
Yugoslavia — prices doubled every 24 hours at the 1994 peak
Germany — prices doubled every 4 days at the 1923 peak
Zimbabwe — prices doubled every 25 hours at the 2008 peak
context: Hungarian pengo inflation reached daily price-doubling. The 100 quintillion pengo note (10^20) was the largest denomination ever printed. The forint replaced the pengo in August 1946; the new currency had to be issued with credible reform to stick.

question: Argentina's 1991 Convertibility Plan pegged the peso 1-to-1 to the US dollar and broke years of inflation. When did this plan collapse?
answer: December 2001 to January 2002, with riots and presidential resignations
choices: December 2001 to January 2002, with riots and presidential resignations
March 1999 — well before the actual collapse
August 2008 — during the global financial crisis
September 2018 — under Macri's IMF stand-by program
context: Five Argentine presidents in two weeks during late 2001. Deposits were frozen (corralito). The peso devalued from 1:1 to 4:1 within months. Savers were wiped out; the middle class was devastated; banking trust took a generation to rebuild.

question: In 2024 Zimbabwe attempted to reintroduce a national currency with a new gold-backed approach. What did they call it?
answer: ZiG — Zimbabwe Gold, gold-backed currency launched April 2024
choices: ZiG — Zimbabwe Gold, gold-backed currency launched April 2024
Bond Notes — earlier failed Zimbabwean monetary experiment
ZWL — older Zimbabwean dollar (Real Time Gross Settlement)
ZIM — earlier short-lived second-generation currency
context: The ZiG is officially backed by gold and forex reserves. Citizens are skeptical, given Zimbabwe's monetary history. Public adoption is still limited; most prices remain quoted in USD. Whether gold-backing this time produces lasting stability remains to be seen.

question: Long-run currency valuation theory holds that exchange rates should equalize the price of a tradeable basket of goods across countries. What is this principle called?
answer: Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) — same goods cost equivalent worldwide
choices: Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) — same goods cost equivalent worldwide
Interest Rate Parity (IRP) — separate FX-forward principle
Covered Interest Parity (CIP) — separate FX-forward principle
Balance of Payments Parity (BOPP) — does not exist as principle.
context: Absolute PPP rarely holds exactly (non-tradeable goods, transportation costs). Relative PPP works better long-term. Big Mac Index, OECD comparative price levels, and IMF PPP-adjusted GDP all rely on this principle. Real exchange rates measure deviations from it.

question: The richest man of the European Renaissance was a German banker who financed kings and emperors from his base in Augsburg. Who?
answer: Jakob Fugger 'the Rich' — banker, mining magnate, Habsburg financier
choices: Jakob Fugger 'the Rich' — banker, mining magnate, Habsburg financier
Cosimo de' Medici — earlier Florentine banker, less wealthy
Jacques Coeur — French royal financier, less wealthy
Andrea Doria — Genoese merchant-prince, separate sphere
context: Fugger financed Maximilian I and Charles V Habsburg, controlled European copper, lent to the Pope, financed the indulgence trade. His estimated peak wealth as share of European GDP exceeds modern billionaires. Sound-money trade enabled this concentration.

question: Isaac Newton, the physicist, also served decades as a senior royal mint official. What was his role?
answer: Master of the Royal Mint from 1699 to 1727, fixing the gold standard
choices: Master of the Royal Mint from 1699 to 1727, fixing the gold standard
Governor of the Bank of England from 1697 to 1715, separate role
Chancellor of the Exchequer briefly from 1714 to 1716
Royal economic adviser without formal Mint position
context: Newton fixed the gold-to-silver ratio in 1717 at a level that over time pulled Britain onto a de facto gold standard. He pursued counterfeiters relentlessly, witnessing executions personally. The physicist-as-monetary-policymaker is a fascinating chapter of monetary history.

question: Pakistan's rupee has steadily depreciated against the dollar across decades. What is the rough scale of decline since 2000?
answer: From around 50 per USD in 2000 to over 280 per USD by 2024
choices: From around 50 per USD in 2000 to over 280 per USD by 2024
From around 5 per USD in 2000 to around 50 per USD by 2024
From around 200 per USD in 2000 to around 1,000 per USD by 2024
