Computers can only count up to 21 million.
The US government set the limit in 2010
Twenty-one is a lucky number for Satoshi.
context: Satoshi chose 21M and a halving schedule to make Bitcoin scarce by design. No central bank can print more. The contrast with fiat money is intentional — sound money in code form.

question: In October 2013 the FBI shut down the Silk Road, an online black market that used Bitcoin. Why does this matter for Bitcoin's history?
answer: It was Bitcoin's first big real-world test of survival.
choices: It was Bitcoin's first big real-world test of survival.
Bitcoin was banned worldwide right after the bust.
Silk Road's bust was Bitcoin's first peak in price.
Silk Road's founders went on to lead the Fed.
context: The Silk Road bust seized hundreds of thousands of BTC. Many predicted Bitcoin's death. Instead it survived and grew. The point: Bitcoin doesn't need its early use cases to keep existing. It runs on its own protocol.

question: In January 2024 the SEC approved spot Bitcoin ETFs for the first time. Why is this a big deal?
answer: Big investors can now hold Bitcoin in normal brokerage accounts.
choices: Big investors can now hold Bitcoin in normal brokerage accounts.
Bitcoin itself was created on this day in January.
The Fed took over the Bitcoin network finally.
Only ten people in the world can now buy it.
context: BlackRock's IBIT and others let pension funds, RIAs, and 401(k)s hold Bitcoin without custody headaches. IBIT hit $10B in 7 weeks — the fastest ETF ever to that mark.

question: Why do many Bitcoin holders use 'hardware wallets' like Trezor or Ledger?
answer: They keep keys offline, safe from hacks and malware
choices: They keep keys offline, safe from hacks and malware
They have larger screens than phones.
They include a Bluetooth tracking chip
They make Bitcoin run twice as fast
context: Software wallets on a phone or PC can be hacked. Hardware wallets store keys in a device that never sees the internet. Sign transactions on the device; broadcast from the PC. Industry standard for serious holders.

question: Bitcoin mining today is dominated by big firms running specialized chips. What are these chips called?
answer: ASICs (Application-Specific Integrated Circuits)
choices: ASICs (Application-Specific Integrated Circuits)
CPUs (Central Processing Units, normal PCs)
GPUs (Graphics Processing Units, gaming)
FPGAs (Field-Programmable Gate Arrays)
context: ASICs do one thing — Bitcoin hashing — incredibly fast. They've replaced GPUs and CPUs entirely for mining. Big mining firms (Marathon, Riot, CleanSpark) run warehouses of ASICs. Energy use is huge.

question: In November 2022, the FTX crypto exchange collapsed. Why was this such a big shock?
answer: It had been valued at $32 billion and seemed safe.
choices: It had been valued at $32 billion and seemed safe.
FTX was the only exchange that ever existed.
Bitcoin itself stopped working after the crash
FTX was owned by the US Treasury secretly.
context: FTX collapsed in days when news broke that customer funds were being used by sister firm Alameda. CEO Sam Bankman-Fried got 25 years. Bitcoin and the network kept working — exchanges fail; the protocol doesn't.

question: In May 2022 the Terra/Luna stablecoin system collapsed. What was the basic problem?
answer: Its 'stable' value relied on a separate coin that crashed
choices: Its 'stable' value relied on a separate coin that crashed
Terra was hacked by foreign government agents.
All Terra users withdrew their coins at once
Terra was outlawed in every major country.
context: Terra's UST stablecoin was 'backed' by Luna — but Luna's price relied on faith in UST. When the loop broke, both crashed to near zero. $40B+ vaporized. Algorithmic stablecoins fell out of fashion fast.

question: Why is El Salvador's adoption of Bitcoin in 2021 a meaningful experiment?
answer: First country to make Bitcoin legal tender alongside the dollar
choices: First country to make Bitcoin legal tender alongside the dollar
El Salvador invented Bitcoin in their nation's bank.
Bitcoin became their only legal money type
El Salvador banned Bitcoin in the same year
context: President Bukele's bet: bring digital money to the unbanked majority. Results so far are mixed but the country still holds Bitcoin on its national balance sheet. Other small nations watch closely.

question: Why do many Bitcoin holders say 'don't trust, verify'?
answer: Anyone can run a node and check the rules themselves.
choices: Anyone can run a node and check the rules themselves.
Trust is the most important part of money.
Bitcoin requires a trusted third party
Verification is illegal in some states.
context: Cypherpunk ethos: don't take anyone's word for it. Run a node, check the chain, verify your transactions. Bitcoin's design lets any user be their own auditor. No middleman required.

question: The US Federal Reserve was created in 1913. Why was it built?
answer: To prevent bank panics like 1907 from happening again
choices: To prevent bank panics like 1907 from happening again
To run the gold mines under Fort Knox
To replace the US Treasury Department
To compete with European central banks
context: The 1907 Panic was halted by JP Morgan personally. Reformers said 'Next time we may not have Morgan.' Within seven years, the Fed was law. The Jekyll Island meeting of 1910 designed the framework.

question: Why is the Fed's choice of interest rates important to the whole economy?
answer: Rates affect every loan, mortgage, and business decision
choices: Rates affect every loan, mortgage, and business decision
Rates are paid only to Fed employees.
Rates pick which states get money
Rates control the price of postage
context: Lower rates encourage borrowing and spending. Higher rates cool things down. Mortgages, car loans, business expansion — all feel Fed rate changes within months.

question: The Federal Reserve has a 'dual mandate' set by Congress in 1978. What two goals must it pursue?
answer: Maximum employment and stable prices
choices: Maximum employment and stable prices
Stable prices and a balanced budget
Maximum employment and free trade
Stable prices and rapid stock growth
context: The Humphrey-Hawkins Act gave the Fed both goals. Critics say they conflict (stagflation in the 1970s). The Bank of England, ECB, and BOJ have narrower mandates focused on inflation alone.

question: Why did Paul Volcker push interest rates above 20% in 1980-81?
answer: To break double-digit inflation, even at the cost of a recession
choices: To break double-digit inflation, even at the cost of a recession
Because banks demanded the high rates first
To match what European central banks did.
To pay off the entire US national debt
context: Volcker took a brutal path to stop the 1970s inflation. Unemployment hit 10.8%. Inflation fell from 14% to 3%. The price was high but the deal stuck for decades. Volcker became the gold standard for Fed chairs.

question: Why is the US dollar the world's main reserve currency today?
answer: Most global trade and savings are priced in dollars.
choices: Most global trade and savings are priced in dollars.
The dollar is the prettiest currency to look at.
It's the heaviest currency in metal coins
All countries must use US dollars by law.
context: Since Bretton Woods (1944), the dollar has been central. Oil, wheat, gold all trade in dollars. Foreign central banks hold US Treasury bonds. This 'dollar dominance' gives the US power but also vulnerability.

question: Why did Nixon close the 'gold window' in August 1971?
answer: Foreign countries were demanding gold faster than the US could provide.
choices: Foreign countries were demanding gold faster than the US could provide.
Gold was banned in the United States that year.
The US ran out of dollars to print.
Nixon owned a private silver mine
context: Foreign central banks (especially France) were trading dollars for US gold. The US gold reserves shrank. Nixon ended dollar-gold convertibility 'temporarily.' It was permanent. The world entered the pure fiat era.

question: Quantitative Easing (QE) is when a central bank:
answer: Buys huge amounts of bonds to push down long-term rates
choices: Buys huge amounts of bonds to push down long-term rates
Raises interest rates to slow inflation down
Prints physical paper money for vending
Hires more economists each quarter
context: QE 1, 2, 3 ran 2008-2014. The Fed's balance sheet went from $900B to $4.5T. Critics say it bailed out asset holders. Defenders argue it averted a deeper depression. Both sides have data.

question: Why did the Fed's balance sheet blow up to about $9 trillion by 2022?
answer: COVID emergency response: it bought trillions of bonds in months
choices: COVID emergency response: it bought trillions of bonds in months
The Fed bought gold from every state's vault
It was a typo on official government forms.
Congress made a one-time gift to the Fed.
context: March 2020: QE was restarted at unprecedented pace. Combined with massive Treasury issuance. The Fed and Treasury moved in near-lockstep. Inflation followed in 2021. The Fed has been trying to shrink the balance sheet since.

question: The European Central Bank (ECB) runs monetary policy for which group of countries?
answer: The 20 EU nations that use the euro
choices: The 20 EU nations that use the euro
Every country in the European Union
All countries in continental Europe
The countries of the Nordic region
context: Not every EU country uses the euro. Sweden, Denmark, Czechia, Poland, Hungary keep their own currencies. The 20 'eurozone' nations share the ECB. Trade-off: currency stability vs. losing local monetary control.

question: Why is the Bank of Japan famous for trying 'unusual' monetary moves?
answer: It has used near-zero rates for decades and pioneered QE.
choices: It has used near-zero rates for decades and pioneered QE.
It is the only bank that uses gold daily.
Japan has zero interest rates only one year.
It only operates on weekends each month
context: Japan went into deflation in the 1990s. The BoJ tried zero rates, then negative rates, then yield-curve control. Inflation finally returned in 2022. Other central banks studied Japan to learn what worked — and what didn't.

question: Jerome Powell, the current Federal Reserve chair, has a background that is unusual for the role. What is his training?
answer: Lawyer and investment banker — not an academic economist
choices: Lawyer and investment banker — not an academic economist
Academic economist from Harvard with PhD
Career US Treasury official for decades
Former CEO of a major US bank firm
context: Powell is the first Fed chair without a PhD in economics in decades. Critics say he leans too heavily on staff models. Defenders praise his communication and pragmatism. He was reappointed by Biden after first appointment by Trump.

question: Why do some economists worry about Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDCs)?
answer: Programmable money could be restricted or even expired by the state.
choices: Programmable money could be restricted or even expired by the state.
CBDCs require everyone to wear special glasses
CBDCs are heavier than physical paper bills.
Only ten people on Earth can use them.
context: China's e-CNY, the ECB's digital euro pilot, and others are running. The state could restrict purchases (no alcohol), set expiry dates (use it or lose it), or freeze accounts. Privacy and freedom concerns are real and growing.

question: Why is the Weimar Germany hyperinflation of 1923 the most-cited example in economics class?
answer: Prices doubled every few days at the peak
choices: Prices doubled every few days at the peak
Germany printed only gold coins that year
The Weimar mark was the strongest currency.
The hyperinflation lasted ten full decades
context: By November 1923 one US dollar bought 4.2 trillion German marks. Workers paid daily and rushed to spend before the morning's wages became worthless by afternoon. Wheelbarrows of cash for a loaf of bread.

question: In 2008 Zimbabwe's central bank issued a 100-trillion-dollar bill. What is the lesson?
answer: A nation printing money without limit destroys its currency
choices: A nation printing money without limit destroys its currency
Bigger bills always make a country richer
Zimbabwe became the world's richest country
The 100-trillion bill was a joke by printers.
context: Zimbabwe's note couldn't buy a loaf of bread. The currency was scrapped; the country uses US dollars now. Same story as Weimar, Hungary 1946, Venezuela 2010s, Lebanon 2020s. Each repeat is somehow a surprise.

question: Why did US inflation hit 9.1% in June 2022?
answer: Trillions in COVID stimulus met broken supply chains
choices: Trillions in COVID stimulus met broken supply chains
Oil prices fell sharply over the year
The Fed raised interest rates too high
Workers refused to take any pay raise
context: $5T+ of pandemic stimulus + bottlenecked ships + Russia's invasion of Ukraine = the highest CPI reading since 1981. Powell had called it 'transitory.' It wasn't. The Fed had to hike aggressively in 2022-2023.

question: Why does inflation hurt people on fixed incomes the most?
answer: Their checks don't keep up with rising prices
choices: Their checks don't keep up with rising prices
Fixed incomes always cause inflation to rise
Fixed-income people own too many bonds
People on fixed incomes love inflation
context: Retirees on fixed pensions, savers with old CDs — their money loses buying power year after year. Workers can ask for raises; people drawing checks can't. Inflation is sometimes called a quiet tax on the elderly.

question: In Argentina, the peso has lost most of its value many times. What pattern keeps repeating?
answer: Government deficits financed by printing money
choices: Government deficits financed by printing money
Foreign powers steal Argentine pesos at night
Argentina has too many gold reserves saved up.
The peso strengthens whenever inflation hits
context: Argentina spends more than it taxes. The central bank prints to cover the gap. Inflation rises. Confidence falls. Crisis. Bailout. Repeat. The pattern dates back to the 1940s and still goes on.

question: Why did the Hungarian pengo set a world inflation record in 1946?
answer: Prices doubled every 15 hours at the peak
choices: Prices doubled every 15 hours at the peak
Pengo notes were the heaviest money ever printed.
Hungary used pengo as the only world currency
Pengo never actually lost any of its value.
context: Hungary's pengo inflation reached daily price-doubling — the worst ever recorded. The 100 quintillion pengo bill (10^20) was the highest denomination ever printed. The forint replaced it later in 1946.

question: In 2019, the Lebanese pound began collapsing after decades of stability. Why?
answer: Lebanese banks had run a Ponzi-like scheme for years.
choices: Lebanese banks had run a Ponzi-like scheme for years.
Lebanon had too much gold in its reserves.
Israel forced Lebanon to print extra money
COVID-19 caused the entire collapse alone
context: Lebanon's banks paid huge interest on dollar deposits, funded by new dollar inflows. When inflows stopped, the system collapsed. The pound lost 98% of its value. Depositors lost dollar savings. A modern Madoff at the national scale.

question: Why is inflation sometimes called a 'hidden tax'?
answer: It quietly cuts the value of your savings without a bill
choices: It quietly cuts the value of your savings without a bill
It is required by law on all paychecks.
It only shows up on paper, not in real life.
It cuts only the value of foreign currency
context: No politician votes 'yes' to take 5% of your savings. But 5% inflation does exactly that. Borrowers gain (repay with cheaper dollars). Savers and lenders lose. The redistribution happens without a single vote.

question: Why did Volcker's high-rate medicine in 1980-82 work to stop inflation?
answer: It cut spending and proved the Fed would defend the dollar.
choices: It cut spending and proved the Fed would defend the dollar.
It increased the money supply to flood the system
It gave free dollars to every American family.
It forced banks to lend more to small firms
context: Rates at 20% killed weak firms and forced everyone to plan around tight money. Inflation crashed from 14% to 3%. Unemployment hit 10.8%. The pain was real. The cure stuck for decades. Volcker became a legend.

question: Why did the 1970s see oil shocks combined with high inflation in the US?
answer: OPEC raised prices and the Fed had printed too much.
choices: OPEC raised prices and the Fed had printed too much.
Cars used too much oil that decade alone
OPEC actually lowered prices that decade
The US had no oil production at all.
context: OPEC's 1973 embargo and 1979 cut spiked oil. The Fed had run loose policy under Burns. Both forces fed into stagflation: high inflation AND high unemployment. The old Keynesian playbook didn't work.

question: The 1990s ran low inflation in the US partly because:
answer: Cheap imports from China and Asia held prices down.
choices: Cheap imports from China and Asia held prices down.
Americans stopped buying any new clothes
The Fed printed money very heavily then
Oil prices climbed quickly each year
context: Trade with China rose dramatically. Cheap goods flowed in. US workers in some sectors lost; consumers gained low prices. The 'China shock' is a real story, debated for fairness, but it kept inflation low for years.

question: Why is the CPI (Consumer Price Index) sometimes criticized as understating inflation?
answer: Its calculation changes have lowered reported numbers over time.
choices: Its calculation changes have lowered reported numbers over time.
CPI counts only food and gas in its basket
CPI is a number picked by a coin flip.
CPI is calculated by foreign agencies only.
context: BLS changed CPI methods multiple times since the 1980s. Critics say each change lowered reported inflation. 'ShadowStats' calculates the old way and finds higher numbers. The debate over the 'true' inflation rate is real.

question: Why did the 1929 stock market crash turn into the Great Depression?
answer: The Fed let the money supply shrink by a third
choices: The Fed let the money supply shrink by a third
Banks made too many small loans that year.
American factories stopped making goods
Foreign nations stopped trading with the US
context: Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz's 1963 book documented this. Banks failed; deposits vanished; money supply fell 1/3. The Fed sat on its hands. Recession became Depression. The lesson: don't let the money supply collapse.

question: During the 1929-33 collapse, what happened to bank deposits in the US?
answer: Thousands of banks failed and depositors lost everything.
choices: Thousands of banks failed and depositors lost everything.
All deposits were insured at full value.
Banks paid extra-high interest to savers
The government printed new money for all
context: About 9,000 US banks failed 1929-33. Deposit insurance (FDIC, 1933) was a response. Today the FDIC covers up to $250K per account. Bank runs are now rare — depositors trust the safety net.

question: Why did Lehman Brothers fail in September 2008?
answer: Heavy bets on mortgage-backed securities went bad fast.
choices: Heavy bets on mortgage-backed securities went bad fast.
Lehman lost all its files in a flood event.
The CEO retired without naming a successor
Lehman was sued by ten thousand workers.
context: Lehman held huge positions in subprime mortgages. As home prices fell, the bonds collapsed. The Fed and Treasury did NOT bail out Lehman. The shock cascaded. AIG was rescued within 48 hours.

question: The TARP (Troubled Asset Relief Program) was a bank bailout signed by which president?
answer: George W. Bush
choices: George W. Bush
Barack Obama
Bill Clinton
Donald Trump
context: October 3, 2008: Bush signed the $700B TARP. The House had voted it down first, then said yes after the Dow dropped 800 points in a day. TARP was repaid; total cost to taxpayers was small. The bailout precedent was huge.

question: Why did Silicon Valley Bank collapse in March 2023?
answer: It bought long-term bonds; rising rates made them lose value.
choices: It bought long-term bonds; rising rates made them lose value.
Hackers stole all of SVB's deposits at once
The bank's founder ran off to Mexico in 2023.
All Silicon Valley startups closed at once
context: SVB held many long-term Treasury bonds bought at low rates. When the Fed hiked rates fast, those bonds fell in value. Depositors realized SVB was underwater. Bank run in days. The FDIC paid all deposits — even those above $250K.

question: Why did the FDIC backstop ALL Silicon Valley Bank deposits — even those above the $250K limit?
answer: Fear of bank-run contagion to other mid-sized banks
choices: Fear of bank-run contagion to other mid-sized banks
The FDIC was required to by US tradition.
SVB had bribed regulators with cash gifts.
FDIC always pays all deposits at any limit
context: The 'systemic risk exception' was invoked. Critics: this extends bailout protection to all big depositors. Defenders: it stopped a wider panic. The precedent matters. Future SVB-style failures will face the same choice.

question: The Panic of 1907 was halted by which private banker?
answer: J.P. Morgan
choices: J.P. Morgan
Andrew Carnegie
John D. Rockefeller
Cornelius Vanderbilt
context: Morgan, then 70, locked top bankers in his library and organized a rescue. The episode showed the US needed an institution, not a private hero. Within seven years the Federal Reserve was created.

question: Northern Rock was the first British bank in over a century to suffer a public bank run. When?
answer: September 2007
choices: September 2007
March 2020
January 1995
May 1850
context: Depositors lined up at branches in Newcastle. The Bank of England nationalized Northern Rock. Bank runs in the UK had seemed impossible in the modern era. The 2008 crisis showed they weren't.

question: Why did First Republic Bank fail in May 2023 even though it served wealthy customers?
answer: Many wealthy depositors had balances above the FDIC limit.
choices: Many wealthy depositors had balances above the FDIC limit.
First Republic only served wealthy California people.
All wealthy people moved out of California suddenly
First Republic was hacked by foreign nations.
context: Many First Republic depositors had millions on deposit. After SVB collapsed, they pulled funds fast. JPMorgan bought the bank at auction. The third major regional failure of spring 2023. Concentration in banking grew.

question: Why did the 2008 crisis become global, not just American?
answer: Mortgage-backed bonds had been sold to banks worldwide.
choices: Mortgage-backed bonds had been sold to banks worldwide.
America banned foreigners from US banks
Other countries had no banking sectors yet.
Foreign banks had no exposure to US loans.
context: Banks in Germany, Iceland, UK, and beyond owned US mortgage bonds. When they went bad, losses hit globally. Iceland's banking sector collapsed; UK nationalized RBS and Lloyds; the Eurozone soon faced its sovereign debt crisis.

question: Henry Ford in the early 1900s did what was then radical for a US factory owner?
answer: Paid workers double the going wage and added a 5-day week
choices: Paid workers double the going wage and added a 5-day week
Hired only relatives from his own family
Refused to make any cars in his factory
Made cars only in red or green colors.
context: Ford's $5-a-day wage (1914) doubled the going rate. He cut shifts from 9 to 8 hours. His goal: keep workers, and let them afford the cars they made. Mass production met mass consumption.

question: Jack Bogle launched the first low-cost retail index fund in 1976 through what company?
answer: Vanguard
choices: Vanguard
Fidelity
Schwab
BlackRock
context: Bogle's First Index Investment Trust was mocked as 'Bogle's Folly.' Today index funds dominate retail investing. He saved ordinary savers trillions in fees over decades. Even Buffett recommends index funds for non-pros.

question: Sam Walton built which retail giant from a single Arkansas store?
answer: Walmart
choices: Walmart
Target
Costco
Kmart
context: Walton opened his first Walmart in 1962 in Rogers, Arkansas. He focused on rural areas, low prices, and efficient supply chains. By the 1990s it was the largest US retailer. The Walton family is among the richest in the world.

question: Warren Buffett famously won a 10-year bet (2008-2017) against hedge funds. The bet was about:
answer: Whether index funds would beat hedge funds after fees.
choices: Whether index funds would beat hedge funds after fees.
Whether the stock market would rise or fall.
Whether gold would beat Bitcoin in returns.
Whether Apple would buy Tesla by 2020.
context: Buffett bet $1M that the S&P 500 index fund would beat a basket of hedge funds. Index returned 7.1%/year; hedge funds 2.2%. The $1M went to Girls Inc. of Omaha. A vivid lesson in passive investing.

question: Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak founded Apple in 1976. Where?
answer: A garage in Los Altos, California
choices: A garage in Los Altos, California
A New York City warehouse
An office in Boston
A factory in Detroit
context: The 'garage' founding myth has some truth — Jobs's parents' garage in Los Altos. The original Apple I sold for $666.66. Apple is now one of the world's most valuable companies.

question: Elon Musk has founded or led which group of companies?
answer: PayPal, Tesla, SpaceX, Neuralink, X
choices: PayPal, Tesla, SpaceX, Neuralink, X
Apple, Microsoft, Google, Amazon
Ford, GM, Chrysler, Tesla
IBM, Intel, AMD, Nvidia
context: Musk's career is unusual: PayPal sale ($165M), Tesla CEO, SpaceX founder, Neuralink, The Boring Company, X (formerly Twitter). Critics and fans both have plenty of material. Few entrepreneurs have spanned so many industries.

question: Jeff Bezos founded Amazon in 1994 selling what online?
answer: Books
choices: Books
Movies
Music CDs
Hardware tools
context: Amazon started as an online bookseller. Books had the easiest catalog to digitize. From there: music, video, electronics, then everything. The 'everything store' model became one of the most disruptive businesses ever.

question: Howard Schultz built which coffee chain into a global giant?
answer: Starbucks
choices: Starbucks
Dunkin'
Tim Hortons
Peet's Coffee
context: Schultz bought Starbucks in 1987 (it was 6 stores then). He pushed the 'Italian café' experience. By 2020 it was 30,000+ stores worldwide. Now a daily routine for millions. Coffee culture in the US changed forever.

question: Larry Page and Sergey Brin met at Stanford and built which search engine?
answer: Google
choices: Google
Yahoo
Bing
Ask Jeeves
context: Google's PageRank algorithm crushed rivals in the late 1990s. The company went public in 2004. Today Alphabet (Google's parent) is one of the most valuable in the world. Two PhD students built it.

question: Madame C.J. Walker, one of America's first self-made female millionaires, built her fortune from:
answer: Hair care products for Black women
choices: Hair care products for Black women
Steel mills in Pittsburgh
Railroad investments in the West
Oil drilling in Texas fields
context: Walker (born Sarah Breedlove, 1867) built her hair care empire in the early 1900s. She employed thousands of women and gave generously to civil rights causes. Her great-great-granddaughter A'Lelia Bundles wrote a famous biography.

question: Mao's 'Great Leap Forward' (1958-62) caused mass deaths from famine. Why?
answer: Forced farms and lies about grain output broke food supply.
choices: Forced farms and lies about grain output broke food supply.
Bad weather lasted ten straight years across China
Foreign nations blocked all food imports for years
Famine swept across all of Asia equally that decade
context: Estimates: 30-45 million deaths from famine. Backyard steel furnaces destroyed farm tools. Officials lied about grain production. The state took 'surplus' that didn't exist.

question: Why did the Soviet Union's planned economy suffer constant shortages?
answer: Without market prices, planners couldn't tell what was needed.
choices: Without market prices, planners couldn't tell what was needed.
Soviet workers refused to make any goods at all
Too many high-quality goods sat unsold each day
Free flights and meals stretched all factories thin
context: Soviet shoppers waited hours for bread, milk, toilet paper. Yet warehouses held tons of unwanted goods. Planners didn't have prices to tell them what to make.

question: Cambodia under the Khmer Rouge (1975-79) carried out what is called:
answer: The Killing Fields — mass execution of city dwellers and intellectuals
choices: The Killing Fields — mass execution of city dwellers and intellectuals
The Great Industrial Leap — fast factory growth
The Year Zero Migration — small village expansion
The Cambodian Renaissance — art and music boom
context: Pol Pot's regime emptied Phnom Penh and killed about 2 million of 8 million Cambodians. Anyone with glasses, education, or city ties was suspect. The 'Killing Fields' remain mass graves visited today. Communism in pure form.

question: Stalin's 1932-33 Holodomor in Ukraine was:
answer: A man-made famine that killed millions of Ukrainians.
choices: A man-made famine that killed millions of Ukrainians.
A natural disaster from drought conditions
A successful agricultural collectivization push
A WWII battle on the eastern front line
context: Stalin's forced grain seizures killed 3-7 million Ukrainians. Borders were sealed; food was confiscated. Ukraine recognizes it as genocide. Many countries today do too. Russia continues to deny it was deliberate.

question: The 1997 'Black Book of Communism' estimated total deaths under communist regimes at:
answer: 65 to 100 million people across the 20th century
choices: 65 to 100 million people across the 20th century
Around 1 million people total
Around 5 million people total
Around 200 million people total
context: The book covers USSR, Mao's China, Cambodia, North Korea, Vietnam, Eastern Europe, Africa, Latin America. Famine, gulag, execution. Critics challenge methodology; mainstream historians accept the broad numbers. Defenders of socialism argue for 'real socialism never tried.'

question: Why did the Berlin Wall come down in 1989?
answer: East Germans fled to West; the regime lost control of the border.
choices: East Germans fled to West; the regime lost control of the border.
East Germany became wealthier than the West
Russia voted to dissolve East German states
The wall fell down from heavy summer rain
context: By 1989, East Germans were leaving through Hungary. Protests grew. On November 9, a confused press conference seemed to announce open borders. Crowds came to the wall; guards stood aside. The wall fell that night.

question: Why did Venezuela's economy collapse in the 2010s under Chavismo?
answer: Price controls and money printing destroyed production.
choices: Price controls and money printing destroyed production.
All the oil ran out completely beneath Venezuela.
Venezuela had no farmers left to grow any food.
Foreign powers blocked Venezuelan trade entirely
context: Hugo Chavez and Maduro nationalized industries, set prices below cost, and printed money. Producers shut down. Stores went empty. Millions of Venezuelans fled. Hyperinflation hit a nation with the world's largest oil reserves.

question: Why did North Korea suffer mass famine in the 1990s?
answer: The end of Soviet aid revealed the system's hollowness
choices: The end of Soviet aid revealed the system's hollowness
Bad weather lasted only a few weeks
North Korea had too many farmers then.
Foreign nations sent too much food aid.
context: The 'Arduous March' famine killed an estimated 600,000 to 2 million. The Soviet collapse cut off subsidies. Industrial farming broke down. Defectors describe eating grass, bark, even people. The regime survived; the people did not.

question: The 'Mises calculation problem' was first published in 1920. What did it predict?
answer: A socialist economy without prices cannot rationally plan
choices: A socialist economy without prices cannot rationally plan
Capitalism would soon collapse from inequality.
Markets would collapse without state planning.
All economies would converge to one model.
context: Mises argued: without market prices for capital goods, planners can't choose between steel-for-cars or steel-for-houses. They guess. The USSR proved Mises right after 70 years of guessing. The argument shaped Hayek's later work.

question: Why did the 1989-91 collapse of Soviet bloc countries vindicate Hayek and Mises?
answer: Decades of warnings about central planning came true exactly.
choices: Decades of warnings about central planning came true exactly.
It proved the Austrian school was wrong.
It showed markets needed more regulation.
It made Marx's predictions come true.
context: Hayek wrote 'Road to Serfdom' in 1944. He warned planning would erode freedom and break economies. By 1991 — Hayek still alive — Eastern Europe was free. He died in 1992 having lived to see his life's work vindicated.

question: The 1971 closing of the gold window matters because:
answer: Currency was no longer tied to anything physical.
choices: Currency was no longer tied to anything physical.
Gold was banned forever in the United States.
All foreign trade with the US stopped that year
The Federal Reserve gained its first chairman
context: Before 1971, dollars could (in theory) be redeemed for gold. After, the dollar floated freely. Inflation soared in the 1970s. Critics argue this fundamentally changed money. Defenders say flexibility was needed.

question: Why did Bretton Woods (1944) set the dollar at $35 per ounce of gold?
answer: It was the rate FDR had set in 1934 after revaluation.
choices: It was the rate FDR had set in 1934 after revaluation.
It was the cost of one ounce of gold then.
Roosevelt picked the number randomly
Foreign nations demanded a higher rate
context: FDR had raised the official gold price from $20.67 to $35 in 1934 — a 41% dollar devaluation. The Treasury made huge bookkeeping profits used to fund the Exchange Stabilization Fund. Bretton Woods locked the $35 rate as the world standard.

question: The Spanish 'piece of eight' silver coin was so important that it became:
answer: The original model for the US dollar
choices: The original model for the US dollar
The currency of every European nation
The only coin used in colonial India
The first coin made of pure gold.
context: Spanish silver dollars (eight reales) dominated global trade from the 1500s to 1850s. American colonists used them daily. The US dollar copied their weight. The '$' sign comes from a stylized P-S for 'pesos.'

question: Sir Isaac Newton served as Master of the Royal Mint. What did he do there?
answer: Fixed the pound to gold at a rate that lasted centuries
choices: Fixed the pound to gold at a rate that lasted centuries
Wrote new physics laws on Mint paperwork.
Made all British coins out of paper.
Issued the first British paper money
context: Newton served from 1699 to 1727. His 1717 gold-silver ratio gradually pulled Britain onto a de facto gold standard. He prosecuted counterfeiters relentlessly. Witnessed executions personally. The physicist-as-monetary-policymaker is a fascinating chapter.

question: Hong Kong has used a 'currency board' system since 1983. What does that mean?
answer: Every HK dollar is backed by US dollar reserves at a fixed rate.
choices: Every HK dollar is backed by US dollar reserves at a fixed rate.
Hong Kong prints US dollars officially
Hong Kong banks all use Bitcoin reserves
Hong Kong uses no paper money anywhere
context: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority must hold USD reserves equal to the HKD in circulation. The peg has survived 1997, 2008, 2020 — but Hong Kong imports US monetary policy with no say. Trade-off: stability vs. local control.

question: Why does the saying 'no free lunch' apply to economics?
answer: Every choice has a cost; someone pays, even unseen.
choices: Every choice has a cost; someone pays, even unseen.
Lunches are always free at most US public schools.
Free lunches exist but only on weekdays in summer
Lunches are usually given out for free by the city.
context: Milton Friedman popularized the phrase. Government 'free' programs are paid by taxpayers. 'Free' shipping is built into the price. Hidden costs are still real costs.

question: Why is 'opportunity cost' one of economics's deepest ideas?
answer: Every choice means giving up the next-best option
choices: Every choice means giving up the next-best option
Costs are always written on a receipt.
Opportunities are free if you ask nicely.
Costs only mean dollars and cents
context: Going to college means not earning that money for 4 years. Buying a car means not buying something else. Time in one job means not in another. Real cost = what you gave up, not what you spent. Hard to teach; harder to apply.

question: 'Tax incidence' is the idea that:
answer: Who pays a tax legally isn't always who really bears it
choices: Who pays a tax legally isn't always who really bears it
Taxes always raise prices by their full amount
Taxes are paid only by big businesses.
Tax law is set by the smallest groups.
context: A payroll tax 'split' between employer and worker is mostly paid by the worker as lower wages. Sales taxes hit consumers if demand is inelastic. The law says who pays; markets decide who really pays. A core concept of tax economics.

question: 'Negative externality' means:
answer: A cost from an action falls on people who didn't choose it
choices: A cost from an action falls on people who didn't choose it
A free benefit goes to people who paid for it
A market price is set higher than the cost.
A buyer pays less than the seller asked
context: Pollution is the classic example. The factory benefits; the village pays in sickness. Solutions: pollution tax, tradable permits, property rights. Each approach has strengths. None are free of cost.

question: Why is the US 'Social Security' system facing a long-term problem?
answer: Fewer workers per retiree than when the system was built.
choices: Fewer workers per retiree than when the system was built.
Social Security pays too little to most retirees
Most Americans refuse to take any benefits
Workers stopped paying into the system
context: When SS started in 1935, 16 workers per retiree. Today it's about 3. By 2034 (per current projections) the Trust Fund runs out for full benefits. Both parties have ducked the reform conversation for decades. The arithmetic doesn't care.

question: Why does most evidence show that rent control reduces the supply of rental housing?
answer: Landlords convert units to condos or refuse to build new rentals
choices: Landlords convert units to condos or refuse to build new rentals
Rent control adds new housing to every block
Tenants stop renting after rent control passes
Cities order more apartments built each year.
context: San Francisco's 2019 study (Diamond, McQuade, Qian) showed exactly this. Controlled buildings got converted. New construction slowed. Net citywide affordability fell. Most economists oppose rent control across the political spectrum.

question: Why does a high minimum wage often reduce jobs for low-skill workers?
answer: Employers can't afford workers whose output is below the wage.
choices: Employers can't afford workers whose output is below the wage.
Minimum wage makes workers smarter quickly
All workers magically learn new skills then
Bosses hire more workers when wages rise
context: If a worker produces $10/hour of value and the boss must pay $15, the boss uses machines, fewer hours, or hires no one. Critics dispute the magnitude. Defenders point to study variation. Most agree some effect exists.

question: Why do hurricane evacuations sometimes see plywood prices double?
answer: Higher prices ration scarce stock to the most urgent uses
choices: Higher prices ration scarce stock to the most urgent uses
Hardware stores enjoy raising prices on storms
Plywood becomes heavier during all hurricanes
Stores must raise prices by law during storms.
context: Without higher prices, first arrivals hoard. Higher prices push casual users to wait. Painful, but it preserves wood for the family with the missing roof. Anti-gouging laws often make shortages worse, not better.

question: Why did 1970s US gas lines form when Nixon imposed price controls on oil?
answer: Below-market prices mean less supply meets more demand
choices: Below-market prices mean less supply meets more demand
Cars stopped working that year completely
OPEC sent extra oil straight to the US.
Americans began walking everywhere
context: Nixon's 1971 price freeze + the 1973 oil embargo caused gas lines for months. Drivers waited hours. Stations rationed. Without the freeze, prices would have risen, demand would have fallen, supply would have come from other sources. Price controls broke the market.

question: Why does a 'price ceiling' below market price create shortages?
answer: Demand exceeds supply at the legal price
choices: Demand exceeds supply at the legal price
Sellers always make more at higher prices
Buyers stop wanting the cheaper item
Ceilings cause prices to skip upward
context: Set the price below where supply meets demand, and buyers want more than sellers offer. Examples: rent control, 1970s gas freeze, Venezuela price controls in the 2010s. Same pattern every time.

question: Why does a 'price floor' above market price create surpluses?
answer: Supply exceeds demand at the legal price
choices: Supply exceeds demand at the legal price
Sellers stop making any product
Floors push prices down naturally
Buyers always want unlimited stuff
context: Minimum wage above market wage = unemployed workers (a surplus of labor). Farm price supports = stockpiles. Set the floor above market clearing, and producers offer more than buyers want.

question: Why do natural disasters often see anti-gouging laws backfire?
answer: Sellers don't ship goods to a region they can't profit in
choices: Sellers don't ship goods to a region they can't profit in
Anti-gouging laws bring more supply quickly
Buyers stop wanting supplies after disasters
Stores must give all goods away for free.
context: If you can't raise the price of a generator past $300 in a hurricane zone, your competitor across state lines won't truck them in. The cap blocks the supply response. Worst outcome: empty shelves at the legal price.

question: Why does the 'cobweb pattern' affect farm prices year after year?
answer: Today's high prices cause oversupply next year
choices: Today's high prices cause oversupply next year
Farmers always plant exactly the right amount
Spider webs control farm market prices
Crop yields stay perfectly stable
context: High soybean prices in 2022 → many farmers plant soy in 2023 → soy glut → low prices in 2023 → fewer plant in 2024 → shortage → high prices in 2024. The cycle repeats. Farm subsidies aim partly to smooth this out.

question: Why does shop floor price discrimination (movies, museums charging less for kids) work?
answer: Different buyers have different willingness to pay.
choices: Different buyers have different willingness to pay.
Kids enjoy movies less than adults do.
Theaters give away kid seats by law
Kids weigh less than full-size adults
context: Charging $12 for adults and $8 for kids fills more seats than $12 for all. Senior discounts, student discounts, day-of-week pricing — all attempts to capture different buyer groups. Standard practice everywhere.

question: Why do many concerts sell out within minutes even when tickets seem cheap?
answer: Artists price below market to keep loyal fans happy
choices: Artists price below market to keep loyal fans happy
Concert tickets are heavy to carry to a sale.
Buyers are scared to pay more for concerts.
The mayor sets all concert prices by law
context: Beyoncé could probably charge $1000/ticket and still sell out. She doesn't, because she values long-term fan goodwill. Resellers grab the difference. The 'real' market price is what fans actually end up paying.

question: In 1920 Ludwig von Mises published an essay that argued socialist economies must fail. What was his core argument?
answer: Without market prices for capital goods, planners can't rationally choose between alternative uses
choices: Without market prices for capital goods, planners can't rationally choose between alternative uses
Workers under socialism would refuse to follow orders from central planners.
Socialist economies lack the technology to build modern factories quickly
Socialist farms can never produce enough food to feed the worker class.
context: Mises's calculation problem: a planner deciding between steel-for-cars or steel-for-houses has no price signal. They guess. The USSR proved him right after 70 years of guessing. Hayek extended the argument to information.

question: Hayek's 1944 'The Road to Serfdom' was published in Britain at a time when most economists favored planning. What was the book's central warning?
answer: Each step toward central control would gradually erode personal freedom.
choices: Each step toward central control would gradually erode personal freedom.
Central planning works when paired with strong leadership
Markets always produce more wealth than planned economies
Government should never collect taxes for any reason at all.
context: The book sold modestly until Reader's Digest published a condensed version in 1945, which sold a million copies. Hayek's argument: planning doesn't just fail economically — it pulls political authority toward authoritarianism.

question: Friedrich Hayek's 1945 essay 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' made what claim about how markets coordinate strangers?
answer: Prices summarize dispersed information that no single planner could collect.
choices: Prices summarize dispersed information that no single planner could collect.
Markets work only when all participants know everything
Central planners outperform markets when given enough data
Trade happens only when buyers and sellers agree on facts
context: A farmer knows his soil; a welder knows her trade. No central office can hold this. Prices condense local knowledge into a number anyone can read. Knock out prices, and the information dies. This is Hayek's deepest argument.

question: In 1937, Ronald Coase published a short paper asking why firms exist if markets are efficient. What was his answer?
answer: Transaction costs — using markets has search, negotiation, and enforcement costs.
choices: Transaction costs — using markets has search, negotiation, and enforcement costs.
Firms exist mainly because of tax advantages from government
Firms exist because workers prefer steady employment
Firms exist due to economies of scale in physical production
context: Coase was 27. The paper became 'The Nature of the Firm' (1937). Firms internalize transactions until the cost of one more in-house equals the cost of one more market contract. The insight won him the 1991 Nobel.

question: Mises's 1949 magnum opus 'Human Action' built economics on what foundational claim?
answer: The action axiom — humans act purposefully, using means toward chosen ends
choices: The action axiom — humans act purposefully, using means toward chosen ends
The labor theory of value developed by Karl Marx
The aggregate supply and demand framework
The principle of comparative national advantage
context: Try to deny the action axiom and you've acted — you've chosen the end of denial. Mises argued this synthetic a priori truth could ground all of economics deductively. Praxeology. Controversial method; powerful insights.

question: In 1971, Hayek won the Nobel Prize. His acceptance speech, 'The Pretence of Knowledge,' attacked what tendency in modern economics?
answer: Treating the economy as something measurable like physics
choices: Treating the economy as something measurable like physics
Using historical data to test economic theories
Publishing economic research in academic journals
Teaching economics to non-PhD students
context: Hayek attacked 'scientism' — the misuse of physics-style precision in social sciences. He argued economists pretend to know more than they can. The speech is required reading for critics of mainstream macro. Still cited today.

question: Murray Rothbard's 1962 'Man, Economy, and State' was originally meant to be:
answer: A textbook summarizing Mises's Human Action for graduate students
choices: A textbook summarizing Mises's Human Action for graduate students
A short pamphlet explaining sound money to citizens
A novel about an Austrian economist's life in America
A children's book introducing free-market ideas to kids
context: Henry Hazlitt commissioned a Human Action textbook from young Rothbard. It grew uncontrollably into a 1000-page Austrian magnum opus. Plus a separate volume, 'Power and Market.' Together they're the Austrian counterpart to mainstream macro textbooks.

question: Frederic Bastiat's parable of the broken window (1850) demonstrates what economic concept?
answer: Opportunity cost — the unseen alternative is always foregone.
choices: Opportunity cost — the unseen alternative is always foregone.
Aggregate demand — broken windows create overall spending
Comparative advantage in window repair specialization
Marginal utility of having backup windows in stock
context: A boy breaks a window. The glazier earns money. Onlookers say: this is good for the economy. Bastiat: no — the shopkeeper would have spent that money on shoes. The shoemaker loses. Society is poorer by one window plus the foregone shoe sale.

question: Friedrich Hayek warned in 'The Fatal Conceit' (1988) about a specific kind of error common among intellectuals. What is it?
answer: Believing humans can design society better than evolved institutions.
choices: Believing humans can design society better than evolved institutions.
Believing markets fail without expert intervention always
Believing democracy can solve every political question.
Believing technology will solve all human problems.
context: Hayek's last book argued that markets, common law, and tradition emerged through trial and error over centuries. Reformers who think they can design something better from scratch usually destroy more than they create. Vintage Hayek.

question: Israel Kirzner, a Mises student now at NYU, developed what concept of entrepreneurship in his 1973 book 'Competition and Entrepreneurship'?
answer: The entrepreneur as alert discoverer of price differentials and unmet needs
choices: The entrepreneur as alert discoverer of price differentials and unmet needs
The entrepreneur as a risk-taker calculating expected returns precisely
The entrepreneur as employer creating jobs for the working class
The entrepreneur as inventor of new technical products only
context: Kirzner's entrepreneur isn't a daredevil — they notice what others miss. A $5 car wash in one town when neighboring towns charge $15. Alertness, not gambling. Disequilibrium is opportunity. Disagrees with Schumpeter on key points.

question: Bitcoin's white paper, published October 31, 2008 by Satoshi Nakamoto, solved what longstanding problem in digital cash?
answer: Double-spending without a trusted central authority
choices: Double-spending without a trusted central authority
Faster transactions than credit card networks
Making digital cash anonymous and untraceable
Reducing the cost of international money transfers
context: The double-spend problem killed every prior digital cash attempt. Satoshi solved it with proof-of-work and a public ledger. The white paper is only 9 pages. Anyone can read it. Bitcoin's first block was mined January 3, 2009.

question: Bitcoin's block subsidy halves about every four years. What was the subsidy when Bitcoin launched, and what is it after the 2024 halving?
answer: 50 BTC → 3.125 BTC after four halvings since launch
choices: 50 BTC → 3.125 BTC after four halvings since launch
100 BTC → 25 BTC after the most recent halving event
1 BTC → 0.5 BTC after each halving since launch
10 BTC → 1 BTC after four halvings since launch
context: Halvings: 2012 (25), 2016 (12.5), 2020 (6.25), 2024 (3.125). Each cuts new supply. By 2140, all 21M coins will exist. After that, miners earn only transaction fees. The schedule is hard-coded; no committee can change it.

question: Bitcoin's mining 'difficulty' adjusts every 2016 blocks. What does it ensure?
answer: Blocks arrive on average every 10 minutes, regardless of total hashpower
choices: Blocks arrive on average every 10 minutes, regardless of total hashpower
Bitcoin's price stays roughly stable across the four-year cycle
Miners share the same amount of profit globally
All countries get equal numbers of new coins
context: When more miners join, blocks come faster. The protocol raises difficulty. When miners leave, difficulty falls. The 10-minute average holds across two-week windows. Genius design — self-regulating without central coordination.

question: A Bitcoin 'multisig' wallet requires multiple signatures to spend. Why do serious holders use them?
answer: Loss of one key doesn't lose the coins; theft of one key doesn't steal them
choices: Loss of one key doesn't lose the coins; theft of one key doesn't steal them
Multisig wallets earn extra Bitcoin from the network
Multisig is required by US law for large holdings.
Multisig speeds up transactions significantly
context: A 2-of-3 multisig means any 2 of 3 keys can spend. Lose one — still have 2. A thief gets one — they have 1 of 3. Hardware wallets like Trezor or Coldcard support multisig. Standard practice for substantial holdings.

question: Bitcoin's Lightning Network, launched 2018, addresses what specific problem with the main chain?
answer: On-chain transactions are too slow and pricey for small everyday payments.
choices: On-chain transactions are too slow and pricey for small everyday payments.
The main chain runs out of new coins for daily transactions
Bitcoin Lightning replaces the main blockchain entirely
Lightning was built by a foreign government secretly.
context: Layer 2: open a channel with someone, send unlimited transactions off-chain at near-zero cost, settle to chain when done. Adopted by Cash App, Strike, Wallet of Satoshi. El Salvador uses Lightning for daily payments.

question: In November 2022, FTX collapsed in days. What had Sam Bankman-Fried been doing with customer funds?
answer: Using them as backstop capital for his trading firm Alameda Research
choices: Using them as backstop capital for his trading firm Alameda Research
Investing them in stocks selected by a financial advisor
Holding them in US Treasury bonds as he had promised.
Donating them to charities focused on global poverty
context: FTX customers thought their crypto was segregated. SBF had been moving billions to Alameda, which was losing money. When users tried to withdraw, the cupboard was bare. SBF got 25 years federal prison. Caroline Ellison cooperated and got 2 years.

question: Bitcoin's '21 million' cap means new coins stop being created around what year?
context: After the 2140 halving, the reward becomes too small to round to satoshis. Miners then earn only transaction fees. Whether fees alone secure the network is debated — but decades remain to find out. The fixed schedule is the point.

question: In May 2010, Laszlo Hanyecz paid 10,000 BTC for two pizzas. At late-2024 prices around $60K/BTC, those coins are now worth:
answer: About $600 million dollars
choices: About $600 million dollars
About $1 million dollars
About $10 million dollars
Less than the cost of the pizzas
context: Bitcoin Pizza Day (May 22) commemorates the first real-world Bitcoin transaction. Hanyecz has said he doesn't regret it — someone had to be first. He paid 41 BTC for pizza again in 2018 over Lightning, then bought more pizzas over various BTC tx types.

question: In 2017, ICOs (Initial Coin Offerings) raised about $5.6B from retail investors. What happened to most of those projects within two years?
answer: Roughly 80% were scams or failed to deliver anything functional.
choices: Roughly 80% were scams or failed to deliver anything functional.
Most projects became successful operating businesses
About 50% returned investor money in full to all buyers
All were converted to Bitcoin by the SEC.
context: Studies put the ICO failure rate at 78-92%. SEC enforcement followed. The era left a generation of retail investors burned and skeptical of 'utility tokens.' Bitcoin survived; most altcoins didn't. The maximalist case rests partly on this record.

question: Why do Bitcoin holders distinguish 'self-custody' from 'exchange custody'?
answer: Self-custody: you hold the keys. Exchange: it's a claim on a firm.
choices: Self-custody: you hold the keys. Exchange: it's a claim on a firm.
Self-custody costs more in fees than exchange custody does.
Exchange custody is illegal in most US states today entirely.
Self-custody requires a special license from the SEC each year.
context: Coins on an exchange (Coinbase, FTX, etc.) live in the exchange's wallet. If it fails or freezes accounts, your claim is worthless. 'Not your keys, not your coins.' Hardware wallets eliminate the counterparty risk.

question: In 1933, FDR's Executive Order 6102 required US citizens to surrender gold to the Federal Reserve at $20.67 per ounce. Within a year, what happened to the official gold price?
answer: Raised to $35 per ounce — a 41% dollar devaluation against gold
choices: Raised to $35 per ounce — a 41% dollar devaluation against gold
Lowered to $10 per ounce as gold became less valuable
Kept at $20.67 for the rest of the 1930s decade.
Eliminated altogether — gold was no longer official money.
context: Americans who complied with EO 6102 lost. The Treasury's bookkeeping profit from revaluation funded the Exchange Stabilization Fund. Private gold ownership stayed illegal until 1975 under Ford. The episode is the founding modern American case of monetary expropriation.

question: From around 300 AD to 1453, the Byzantine Empire minted a gold coin that held remarkably stable weight and purity. What was it called?
answer: The solidus — 4.5 grams of gold, stable for over 700 years
choices: The solidus — 4.5 grams of gold, stable for over 700 years
The denarius — Roman silver coin, debased away by 300 AD
The florin — Florentine gold coin from the 1200s
The ducat — Venetian gold coin from the 1200s
context: The solidus is the longest-running sound money in history. Western Europe imitated it as the 'bezant.' Stable money attracted commerce; commerce funded Byzantium's resilience. The eventual debasement under Alexios I (~1080) marked the empire's decline.

question: In the 1500s through 1800s, Spanish silver coins from Mexican and Peruvian mines dominated global trade. The US dollar was modeled on which Spanish coin?
answer: The piece of eight (real de a ocho) — 8 reales, ~27 grams of silver
choices: The piece of eight (real de a ocho) — 8 reales, ~27 grams of silver
The doubloon — Spanish gold coin worth multiple silver pesos
The maravedi — Spanish copper coin of small value
The escudo — Spanish gold coin used for large trades
context: The Spanish dollar's scoring let it be broken into eight reales — hence 'two bits' for a quarter. American colonists used them. The US Mint Act of 1792 defined the dollar to match the Spanish coin's silver content. The '$' sign comes from a stylized P-S.

question: In 1717 the British physicist Isaac Newton, as Master of the Royal Mint, fixed the gold-silver ratio. What was the long-term effect?
answer: Britain drifted onto a de facto gold standard that lasted until 1914
choices: Britain drifted onto a de facto gold standard that lasted until 1914
Britain demonetized gold and went onto pure silver standard.
British coins were melted down for use in scientific work.
The pound was banned in continental Europe for a decade.
context: Newton's rate slightly overvalued gold relative to silver in Britain. Silver flowed out; gold stayed. Britain accidentally became a gold-standard country. The framework lasted through the Industrial Revolution and Pax Britannica. The physicist as monetary policymaker.

question: The Coinage Act of 1873 demonetized silver in the US. Silver advocates later called it:
answer: The Crime of '73 — silver demonetization by stealth
choices: The Crime of '73 — silver demonetization by stealth
The Great Silver Reform — beneficial currency modernization
The Bimetallic Compromise — fair gold-silver balance
The Sherman Act — anti-monopoly silver regulation
context: Silver miners and inflation-leaning farmers viewed the act as a banker's conspiracy. It fueled the Free Silver movement that produced Bryan's 1896 'Cross of Gold' speech. Mainstream historians dispute the conspiracy framing; the political resentment was real.

question: In August 1971, President Nixon ended dollar-gold convertibility. The change is called the:
answer: Nixon Shock
choices: Nixon Shock
Reagan Reset
Carter Cut
Bretton Crash
context: Nixon's televised announcement on August 15, 1971 'temporarily' suspended gold convertibility. The temporary became permanent. The world entered the pure fiat era. Currencies floated against each other, anchored to nothing. Inflation soared in the 1970s.

question: The Bank of England, founded in 1694, is the world's oldest continuously operating central bank. What was its original purpose?
answer: Fund King William III's war against France via private notes
choices: Fund King William III's war against France via private notes
Regulate British banks to prevent panic and runs
Coin silver and gold for the British Crown
Provide banking services to British citizens
context: The BoE began as a private company lending £1.2M to the Crown for a monopoly on London note issuance. War finance birthed central banking. The framework allowed governments to monetize debt — the template followed worldwide.

question: In November 1910, six men met secretly at Jekyll Island, Georgia. They drafted what became the Federal Reserve. The senator who led was:
answer: Nelson Aldrich — Senate Banking, Rockefeller's son-in-law
choices: Nelson Aldrich — Senate Banking, Rockefeller's son-in-law
Henry Cabot Lodge — Massachusetts senator, foreign policy
Robert La Follette — Wisconsin progressive, opposed the plan
Carter Glass — actually a House member, not at the meeting
context: Aldrich led. Paul Warburg and Frank Vanderlip of Rockefeller bank, Henry Davison and Charles Norton of Morgan, Treasury official A. Piatt Andrew rounded out the group. They posed as duck hunters and used first names only. The meeting's existence wasn't widely known for over a decade.

question: From 1923 to 1931, German hyperinflation peaked in November 1923 when one US dollar bought how many German marks?
answer: About 4.2 trillion marks at the worst point
choices: About 4.2 trillion marks at the worst point
About 4.2 thousand marks at the worst point
About 4.2 million marks at the worst point
About 4.2 hundred marks at the worst point
context: From 4.2 marks per dollar in 1914 to 4.2 trillion in November 1923. A 12-order-of-magnitude collapse. Workers paid daily. The Rentenmark stabilization (1923-24) was treated as an economic miracle. Weimar's social damage helped fuel later political extremism.

question: In 1946 Hungary set the all-time inflation record. At peak, prices doubled how often?
answer: Every 15 hours
choices: Every 15 hours
Every 15 days
Every 15 weeks
Every 15 months
context: The Hungarian pengo's collapse produced the 100 quintillion pengo note (10^20) — the largest denomination ever printed anywhere. The forint replaced the pengo in August 1946. New currency, credible reform, stabilization. The Hungarian record still stands as the worst recorded hyperinflation.

question: Paul Volcker took over the Federal Reserve in 1979 with inflation running above 11%. By 1980-81 he had pushed the federal funds rate to:
answer: Above 19% — the highest in Fed history
choices: Above 19% — the highest in Fed history
About 10% — modestly above prior cycle highs
About 5% — moderate tightening
Above 50% — emergency war-time levels
context: Volcker's tough medicine broke the 1970s inflation. Unemployment hit 10.8%. Mortgage rates topped 18%. Inflation fell from 14% to 3% by 1983. Politically painful but durably effective. Volcker became the benchmark for tough Fed chairs.

question: Alan Greenspan served as Fed chairman from 1987 to 2006. What is the central criticism of his tenure?
answer: Easy money fueled tech and housing bubbles that burst after he left.
choices: Easy money fueled tech and housing bubbles that burst after he left.
He raised interest rates too aggressively in every cycle
He refused to provide liquidity during financial crises
He targeted high inflation as a deliberate policy goal
context: Greenspan cut rates after LTCM (1998), after 9/11, and held them low into 2004. Critics (Austrians especially) say this fueled dot-com and housing bubbles. He was praised as 'Maestro' through 2007. The 2008 crash sharply revised his legacy. He acknowledged a 'flaw' in his model in October 2008.

question: Ben Bernanke, Fed chair 2006-2014, was a Great Depression scholar before joining the Fed. What was his core academic claim about 1929-33?
answer: The Fed's failure to provide liquidity turned recession into Depression
choices: The Fed's failure to provide liquidity turned recession into Depression
The 1929 stock crash directly caused the Depression
Tariffs alone caused the global Depression of the 1930s
Bank deposits were too high before the 1929 crash.
context: Bernanke built on Friedman-Schwartz (1963): the Fed let M2 collapse 1/3 in 1929-33. Thousands of banks failed. He vowed in 2002 not to repeat the mistake. In 2008-09 he launched QE on this principle. Critics on the right argue QE has its own costs.

question: Under Chair Bernanke in January 2012, the Federal Reserve adopted what specific inflation target measured by PCE?
answer: 2 percent — chosen to allow flexibility without harming the dollar's credibility
choices: 2 percent — chosen to allow flexibility without harming the dollar's credibility
1 percent — chosen to be near-zero without risk of deflation.
3 percent — chosen to allow faster nominal wage growth
0 percent — chosen for strict price stability mandates
context: The 2% target had been the global standard since New Zealand pioneered it in 1989. Bernanke formalized it for the Fed. Austrian and gold-standard critics prefer lower targets. The Fed shifted to 'flexible average' targeting in 2020.

question: Jerome Powell's 'transitory' framing of 2021 inflation was retired in late November 2021. By that point, US CPI inflation had risen to:
answer: About 6.8% — well above the Fed's 2% target
choices: About 6.8% — well above the Fed's 2% target
About 2.3% — within the Fed's target range
About 12.5% — above the actual peak of the cycle
About 0.5% — actually well below target
context: Powell's 'transitory' lasted from spring 2021 to November 30, 2021, when he retired the term in Senate testimony. By then CPI was 6.8%. The Fed didn't begin raising rates until March 2022, with CPI at 8.5%. The 'too slow' charge is the central Fed critique of the 2020s era.

question: Between March 2022 and July 2023, the Fed raised the funds rate from 0-0.25% to a peak that held through 2024. What was the peak?
answer: 5.25 to 5.5 percent — the most aggressive cycle since Volcker
choices: 5.25 to 5.5 percent — the most aggressive cycle since Volcker
10.0 to 10.25 percent — Volcker-era levels not reached
2.50 to 2.75 percent — modest tightening
20.0 to 20.25 percent — unprecedented restriction
context: The fastest hiking cycle in basis-points-per-month since the early 1980s. By mid-2023 the rate hit 5.25-5.5%. The Fed held through September 2024 before beginning to cut. Inflation slowly fell to roughly 3%. Whether 2024 was a true 'soft landing' or delayed pain is still debated.

question: The Federal Reserve operates under a 'dual mandate' set by the Humphrey-Hawkins Act. The mandate specifies what two goals?
answer: Maximum employment and stable prices
choices: Maximum employment and stable prices
Stable prices and balanced US trade
Maximum employment and stable exchange rates
Stable prices and financial stability only
context: The dual mandate is unusual among major central banks. The ECB and BOJ focus on price stability alone. The Fed must respond to both inflation AND unemployment indicators. Critics argue the two goals can conflict — particularly in stagflation, where managing one worsens the other.

question: In March 2020, the Fed launched unprecedented facilities including buying corporate bonds for the first time. Why did this matter so much?
answer: It crossed the line from government debt to private debt purchases
choices: It crossed the line from government debt to private debt purchases
It only continued the same policies as before
It was a small program that ended quickly.
It applied only to foreign companies that month
context: PMCCF and SMCCF facilities. Hayek would have called this intervention at the heart of price discovery. Defenders say the moves prevented a 1930s-style collapse. Critics say they cemented moral hazard at corporate scale. Both sides have evidence.

question: Between 2020 and 2022 the Federal Reserve's balance sheet expanded dramatically. What was the rough peak?
answer: About $9 trillion — roughly 40% of US GDP
choices: About $9 trillion — roughly 40% of US GDP
About $1 trillion — slightly above pre-2008 levels
About $50 trillion — far above any historical level
About $200 billion — below pre-2008 levels
context: Pre-2008: $900 billion. Post-2014 QE: $4.5T. 2020-22 surge: $9T. The Fed and Treasury moved in near-lockstep — fiscal-monetary coordination at unprecedented scale. The Fed has tried to shrink the balance sheet since 2022 with mixed success.

question: In June 2024 the Supreme Court overturned the 1984 Chevron doctrine in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo. What changed?
answer: Federal agencies no longer get automatic deference for interpreting laws
choices: Federal agencies no longer get automatic deference for interpreting laws
All federal regulations were declared unconstitutional.
Congress took over all agency rulemaking immediately.
The Federal Reserve lost its operational independence.
context: Chevron (1984) had let agencies interpret ambiguous statutes. Courts deferred. Loper Bright (2024) restored courts as final interpreters. Major shift in administrative state's power. The Federalist Society's decades-long strategy bore fruit. Implications still unfolding.

question: Why did Silicon Valley Bank collapse in March 2023, despite being a large and seemingly well-run bank?
answer: Bought long-duration Treasuries at low rates; the Fed's hikes destroyed bond values.
choices: Bought long-duration Treasuries at low rates; the Fed's hikes destroyed bond values.
Hackers breached SVB's security and stole customer funds
Founder fraud diverted billions to offshore accounts
All tech startups withdrew on the same coordinated day
context: SVB's bond portfolio lost 20%+ in market value as rates rose. Tech depositors realized this. Twitter sped the run. $42 billion withdrawn in a single day. The FDIC backstopped all deposits — including above the $250K limit — under the systemic risk exception. Precedent matters.

question: On October 24, 1929 ('Black Thursday') and Tuesday October 29, the NYSE saw massive selling. What is the dominant Friedman-Schwartz interpretation of why the crash became the Great Depression?
answer: The Fed let the money supply contract by a third as banks failed
choices: The Fed let the money supply contract by a third as banks failed
Tariff war alone caused the global economic collapse
Federal stimulus spending was too small in 1930.
The gold standard had no role in deepening the slump.
context: Friedman and Schwartz's 1963 'Monetary History of the United States' became the standard account. Bank failures destroyed deposits. The Fed sat on its hands. Recession became Depression. Bernanke applied the lesson in 2008-09 with massive liquidity provision.

question: The 2008 Lehman Brothers bankruptcy was the largest in US history. The Fed and Treasury chose NOT to bail it out — unlike Bear Stearns six months earlier. Why?
answer: Political pressure plus the absence of a willing private buyer
choices: Political pressure plus the absence of a willing private buyer
Lehman was too small for systemic risk concern.
Lehman had no exposure to mortgage-backed securities.
The Treasury had unlimited funds and unlimited authority.
context: Bernanke and Paulson have given multiple explanations. Treasury argued it lacked clear legal authority to lend to Lehman. Critics argue moral hazard motives. The result: bankruptcy filing September 15, 2008. $639 billion in assets. AIG bailout began within 48 hours.

question: In October 1907, a financial panic threatened to bring down major NYC banks. With no central bank, the rescue was led personally by:
answer: J.P. Morgan — locked top bankers in his library until they agreed
choices: J.P. Morgan — locked top bankers in his library until they agreed
Andrew Carnegie — used his steel fortune to backstop
John D. Rockefeller — used Standard Oil profits
Cornelius Vanderbilt — used his railroad fortune
context: Morgan was 70 years old. He marshaled a private rescue from his Madison Avenue library. The 1907 Panic became the political pretext for creating the Federal Reserve. Senator Aldrich led the National Monetary Commission that culminated at Jekyll Island in 1910.

question: During the 2008 crisis, the TARP (Troubled Asset Relief Program) was authorized at what initial size?
answer: $700 billion (later reduced to $475 billion)
choices: $700 billion (later reduced to $475 billion)
$70 billion — actually a much smaller program
$7 trillion — actually much larger than reality
$7 billion — far below the actual program
context: TARP was signed by Bush on October 3, 2008 after an initial House rejection sent the Dow down nearly 800 points. The headline was $700B; Dodd-Frank later capped it at $475B. Final program cost to taxpayers was small (~$30B). The political precedent was enormous.

question: In March 2008, Bear Stearns collapsed in a classic shadow-banking run. The Fed-arranged Sunday-night sale to JPMorgan Chase was initially at:
answer: $2 per share (later raised to $10 after pushback)
choices: $2 per share (later raised to $10 after pushback)
$15 per share — a more market-aligned price
$30 per share — close to recent trading range
$172 per share — Bear's price a year earlier
context: JPMorgan initially agreed to $2; outraged Bear shareholders forced a renegotiation to $10. Bear had traded at $172 a year earlier. The Fed took $30B of Bear's worst assets via the Maiden Lane vehicle. The Bear deal foreshadowed the September crisis.

question: Why is 'moral hazard' a serious concern when governments bail out failing banks?
answer: Bankers may take more risks if they expect future bailouts.
choices: Bankers may take more risks if they expect future bailouts.
Bailouts are kind acts that hurt nobody at all.
Banks pay back every dollar with no taxpayer cost
Moral hazard means banks always behave morally
context: Heads I win, tails taxpayers lose. The 2008 bailouts set a precedent that the largest US banks understood. Some economists argue this set up later crises. The cure debated: let bad banks fail; protect depositors only. Politics rarely permits the cure.

question: Why did Iceland's three major banks all collapse in October 2008, devastating the country?
answer: Their foreign-currency liabilities far exceeded national reserves
choices: Their foreign-currency liabilities far exceeded national reserves
Iceland had banned international banking that year.
All Icelandic banks were US subsidiaries that failed.
Iceland had recently joined the euro and could not print.
context: Glitnir, Landsbanki, Kaupthing — combined assets 10x Icelandic GDP. They borrowed dollars and euros heavily. When the GFC froze interbank lending, they had no central-bank lender of last resort big enough to save them. Iceland defaulted, devalued, and restructured. Painful but ultimately recovered.

question: Northern Rock, in September 2007, suffered the first major British bank run in over a century. Why?
answer: It relied on wholesale short-term funding that dried up suddenly
choices: It relied on wholesale short-term funding that dried up suddenly
It was bought by a foreign government secretly.
Its CEO was caught stealing from customer accounts.
Most depositors were over the FDIC limit then.
context: Northern Rock had borrowed short and lent long. The 2007 credit freeze killed its funding model. Queues outside Newcastle branches. The Bank of England nationalized it. The first vivid sign that the US subprime crisis was global.

question: Why does each major banking crisis tend to expand the powers and balance sheet of the central bank that follows?
answer: Each crisis is met by new emergency tools that become permanent.
choices: Each crisis is met by new emergency tools that become permanent.
Crises always reduce central bank powers over time
Crises have no impact on central bank size.
Central banks are abolished after each major crisis.
context: 1907 → Federal Reserve (1913). 1929 → FDIC, Glass-Steagall. 2008 → emergency facilities, expanded balance sheet. 2020 → corporate bond buying. The ratchet only goes one way. Each crisis grows the institution. Reformers (Selgin, White, Hummel) propose alternatives — none have prevailed.

question: James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock's 1962 'The Calculus of Consent' founded the field of public choice. What is the central insight?
answer: Politicians and voters are self-interested actors, like consumers in markets.
choices: Politicians and voters are self-interested actors, like consumers in markets.
Politicians are uniquely public-spirited compared to private actors.
Markets are inherently corrupt and need political guidance.
Voters always make the best collective decisions possible
context: Buchanan won the 1986 Nobel. The field treats government decisions through the same lens as market decisions: self-interest plus incentives plus constraints. The implication: many government failures are predictable, not accidents.

question: Gordon Tullock's 1967 paper introduced what concept that explains lobbying, licensing, and political privilege?
answer: Rent seeking — spending real resources to capture politically created profits.
choices: Rent seeking — spending real resources to capture politically created profits.
Capture theory — agencies become tools of the industries they regulate
Public goods — items markets cannot provide because of free riding
Median voter — politicians pander to the middle of the distribution
context: Anne Krueger named it 'rent seeking' in 1974. Tullock's insight: monopoly costs include not just the deadweight triangle but resources spent to obtain the monopoly. Lobbying, campaign donations, revolving doors — all pure social losses. Explains a lot of modern Washington.

question: Why does 'regulatory capture' tend to happen at federal agencies like the SEC, FDA, and FCC over time?
answer: Industry funds campaigns, places alumni at agencies, and writes friendly rules
choices: Industry funds campaigns, places alumni at agencies, and writes friendly rules
Regulators always serve only the public interest properly
Agencies operate independent of any political process
Industries have no relationship with their regulators.
