context: Stigler's 1971 paper formalized capture theory. Pattern: regulators come from industry, return to industry. Each cycle softens rules. Public is dispersed and unorganized; industry is concentrated and well-funded. The math favors capture over the long run.

question: Mancur Olson explained why small groups often beat large ones politically. What is his key insight?
answer: Small concentrated groups overcome collective-action problems easier than large groups
choices: Small concentrated groups overcome collective-action problems easier than large groups
Large groups have more votes and always win elections.
Politicians ignore small groups in favor of large groups
All groups have equal influence in modern democracies.
context: Olson's 'Logic of Collective Action' (1965). Smaller groups can monitor members; large groups face free-rider problems. Each sugar farmer cares about tariffs; each shopper barely notices. Sugar farmers organize and lobby; shoppers don't. Asymmetric organization beats asymmetric numbers.

question: Why is 'crony capitalism' attacked by critics on both the left and the right?
answer: Both see it as firms gaining wealth via political favors, not market service
choices: Both see it as firms gaining wealth via political favors, not market service
Both see it as a sign of healthy competition working well
Both blame it on small businesses cheating the system
Both see it as the same thing as ordinary capitalism
context: Bernie Sanders and Tom Massie agree on this. Crony capitalism = bailouts, subsidies, sweetheart contracts. The 2008 bank bailouts. Solyndra. Sugar tariffs. Big pharma's regulatory moats. The principled left and the libertarian right share the diagnosis if not the cure.

question: Why has occupational licensing grown from about 5% to about 25% of US workers since 1960?
answer: Licensed practitioners lobby states to protect themselves from competition
choices: Licensed practitioners lobby states to protect themselves from competition
Modern jobs are inherently more dangerous than before.
Consumers demand licensing in every occupation possible
Licensing requirements are set by federal law uniformly.
context: Hair braiders, interior designers, casket sellers, tour guides — licensing has expanded enormously. Most licensing benefits incumbents (Stigler), not consumers. The Institute for Justice has won multiple constitutional challenges. The Cantillon effect of licensure-protected wages is real.

question: Why does the FDA's drug-approval process tend toward over-caution rather than balanced risk?
answer: Visible victims of bad drugs are political; invisible victims of delayed good drugs aren't.
choices: Visible victims of bad drugs are political; invisible victims of delayed good drugs aren't.
The FDA has perfect information about all drug effects each day.
Drug makers have no influence over the FDA approval process at all.
FDA officials are immune to political pressure from all groups.
context: Henry Miller's work documents the asymmetric political economics. A drug that hurts someone makes the news. A drug delayed for years kills people invisibly — they were sick longer or died. Bureaucratic incentives favor over-cautious approvals.

question: In Public Choice theory, why might a small interest group (sugar farmers, taxi medallion holders) consistently beat a large interest group (consumers, would-be drivers) politically?
answer: Smaller groups can organize collective action more easily.
choices: Smaller groups can organize collective action more easily.
Larger groups always win in democratic politics
Government policy is decided by random chance.
Voters in the majority always know all policies
context: Mancur Olson's 'The Logic of Collective Action' (1965). Small groups overcome free-rider problems. Each member's stake is large enough to lobby. Large groups face huge coordination costs. Each consumer's stake in any one policy is small. Asymmetric organization = asymmetric power.

question: Why is 'public choice' analysis sometimes called 'politics without romance'?
answer: It treats politicians as self-interested rather than uniquely virtuous
choices: It treats politicians as self-interested rather than uniquely virtuous
It assumes politicians never act in public interest at all
It ignores the role of voters in democracy entirely
It claims private markets are always better than government.
context: Buchanan's phrase. Public choice doesn't say politicians are bad people. It says they respond to incentives like everyone else. The implication: institutional design matters. Reduce the gains from rent-seeking and you'll get less rent-seeking, regardless of which party holds office.

question: Why does the 'principal-agent problem' apply to elected officials?
answer: Voters (principals) can't perfectly monitor what officials (agents) do.
choices: Voters (principals) can't perfectly monitor what officials (agents) do.
Officials always serve voter interests perfectly automatically
There is no relationship between voters and officials.
Voters give officials specific written instructions daily
context: Voters can't read every bill, attend every hearing, or track every vote. Officials can pursue their own interests within the gap. Solutions: term limits, sunshine laws, gerrymandering reform, single-issue voters — none perfect. The gap is structural. Smaller government means smaller gap.

question: Joseph Schumpeter's 1942 'Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy' introduced what concept of dynamic economic change?
answer: Creative destruction — innovation constantly destroying existing positions
choices: Creative destruction — innovation constantly destroying existing positions
Stable equilibrium — markets always tend toward balanced states
Random walks — economic change is unpredictable noise.
Government-managed competition — antitrust ensures dynamism
context: Schumpeter: monopolies are temporary in a healthy economy because rivals invent new technologies. AT&T was destroyed by VoIP. Kodak by digital. Blockbuster by Netflix. The dynamic Austrian-Schumpeterian view differs sharply from static-equilibrium analysis.

question: Frank Knight's 1921 'Risk, Uncertainty, and Profit' distinguished risk from uncertainty in a way that defined modern entrepreneurship theory. What is the distinction?
answer: Risk has knowable probabilities; uncertainty does not.
choices: Risk has knowable probabilities; uncertainty does not.
Risk is small; uncertainty is large.
Risk applies only to insurance; uncertainty to investing
Risk and uncertainty are the same concept exactly.
context: Knight: a coin flip has known probabilities (risk). The success of a startup, a new product, a new political regime has no known distribution (uncertainty). Insurance markets handle risk. Entrepreneurial profit comes from bearing true uncertainty. The framework underlies modern Austrian and Knightian thought.

question: Israel Kirzner's contribution to Austrian theory was framing the entrepreneur as:
answer: Alert discoverer of price differentials and unmet needs
choices: Alert discoverer of price differentials and unmet needs
Calculated risk-taker with insurance against losses
Employer-creator of jobs for working-class workers
Inventor of new physical products and technology only
context: Kirzner's 1973 book argued the entrepreneur isn't a daredevil but someone who notices what others miss. A $5 car wash where neighboring towns charge $15. Alertness, not gambling. Markets are constantly in disequilibrium; entrepreneurs close the gaps. Connects classical economics to real business practice.

question: US Small Business Administration data shows what fraction of new firms survive five years?
answer: About 50 percent — half close, half are still operating after five years.
choices: About 50 percent — half close, half are still operating after five years.
About 95 percent — almost all survive their first five years
About 10 percent — only one in ten survive five years
About 80 percent — most survive their first five years
context: SBA tracks this carefully. The 50% number has been remarkably stable across decades. Reasons for failure: undercapitalization, no clear customer fit, bad pricing, slow to adapt, founder burnout. Survivors learn faster than competitors. Entrepreneurship is fundamentally about learning from failure.

question: Why is 'cash flow' often more important than 'profitability' for small businesses?
answer: A profitable business can still fail if cash runs out before revenue arrives.
choices: A profitable business can still fail if cash runs out before revenue arrives.
Cash flow is the same thing as profitability exactly.
Profitability has no relationship to business survival.
Cash flow only matters for very large businesses
context: Classic case: pay supplier today, customer pays in 60 days. Even with positive accounting profit, you can run out of cash. Many growing firms fail this way. Cash management is the daily lifeblood. The biggest cause of small-business death isn't bad ideas — it's running out of cash.

question: Why do successful entrepreneurs often emphasize 'finding a niche' rather than competing in big markets?
answer: Less competition and more focused customer needs in niches
choices: Less competition and more focused customer needs in niches
Niches always pay more than big markets
All big markets are closed to new entrants.
The government requires niche businesses to start
context: A small gym in a rural town has no rival; a gym in Manhattan fights ten others. Peter Thiel's 'Zero to One' makes this argument explicitly. Monopoly-like positions in niches are valuable. Competition in commodity markets compresses margins to zero. Find the gap. Fill it. Scale up.

question: Henry Ford's 1914 $5-a-day wage was famous because it:
answer: Doubled the going rate and cut worker turnover
choices: Doubled the going rate and cut worker turnover
Was required by federal labor law that year.
Was actually below the prevailing market wage.
Was a tax dodge to lower factory profits.
context: Ford's economics worked: workers stayed longer, productivity rose, training costs fell. The 'workers can afford the cars they make' line was both PR and reality. Critics on the right argue the wage was sustainable only because of Ford's mass-production efficiencies.

question: Why did Jack Bogle's Vanguard 500 Index Fund (1976) revolutionize retail investing?
answer: Low fees and broad diversification beat most active managers over time
choices: Low fees and broad diversification beat most active managers over time
It promised guaranteed returns higher than any other fund
It invested in only one company at a time
It required minimum $1 million investment from buyers
context: Initially mocked as 'Bogle's Folly' — settling for average. Decades of evidence: most active managers underperform after fees. Bogle saved retail investors trillions of dollars. Even Warren Buffett recommends index funds for non-pros. Bogle died 2019; index funds are now dominant.

question: Why has the venture capital model produced both spectacular successes and many failures?
answer: VCs bet on many startups expecting most to fail and a few to win huge
choices: VCs bet on many startups expecting most to fail and a few to win huge
VCs only invest in guaranteed success companies
VCs never lose money on any of their investments
VCs invest only in established mature companies
context: Power-law distribution: a fund's returns come from a tiny number of huge winners. Most investments return zero. Sequoia, Andreessen Horowitz, Benchmark — even top funds have many losses. The model works because the winners are so large. Doesn't work for funding small or stable businesses.

question: Why is the United States consistently ranked among the world's most entrepreneurial countries?
answer: Bankruptcy law forgives failed founders and lets them try again
choices: Bankruptcy law forgives failed founders and lets them try again
American workers are smarter than workers anywhere else.
The US government picks winners and funds them all
Other countries have no startup culture at all.
context: Chapter 7 lets you walk away from business debts. In some other countries, bankruptcy follows you for life. Add cheap incorporation (Delaware), deep capital markets, and a cultural tolerance for failure. The recipe for retry, retry, retry until something works.

question: Argentina's 1991 Convertibility Plan pegged the peso 1-to-1 to the US dollar. Why did it collapse in late 2001?
answer: Fiscal deficits and rigid peg created unsustainable buildup of pressure.
choices: Fiscal deficits and rigid peg created unsustainable buildup of pressure.
Foreign investors successfully attacked the Argentine reserves
Argentina was conquered militarily by neighboring countries.
Argentina chose to abandon the dollar peg voluntarily and easily
context: Five presidents in two weeks during late 2001. Deposits frozen (corralito). Peso devalued from 1:1 to 4:1 within months. Savers wiped out. The middle class devastated. The country defaulted on $93 billion in sovereign debt. Recovery took years; trust took a generation.

question: Why did Lebanon's pound collapse beginning in October 2019, after decades of de facto stability?
answer: Lebanese banks had run a Ponzi-like dollar scheme that finally exploded.
choices: Lebanese banks had run a Ponzi-like dollar scheme that finally exploded.
An earthquake destroyed all Lebanese financial reserves.
Foreign sanctions cut off all Lebanese trade overnight
Lebanon's central bank had been honest and well-managed.
context: Riad Salameh ran the Banque du Liban for 30 years. The system paid high interest on dollar deposits, funded by new inflows. When inflows stopped, the cupboard was bare. The lira lost 98% of its value. Depositors lost most of their dollar savings. The Ponzi structure had been hiding in plain sight.

question: Zimbabwe's hyperinflation peaked in 2008. The Reserve Bank issued a 100-trillion-dollar bill that couldn't buy a loaf of bread. What ended the inflation?
answer: Adopting the US dollar and other foreign currencies for daily use
choices: Adopting the US dollar and other foreign currencies for daily use
Strict price controls enforced by the army
Printing more zeroes on existing currency bills
Voluntary spending freeze by all citizens together
context: By 2009 Zimbabwe abandoned its currency. Multi-currency regime (USD, ZAR, GBP) brought stability. The 2024 ZiG (Zimbabwe Gold) tried gold-backing again with limited adoption. The lesson: stopping a hyperinflation requires credible monetary reform, not just slower printing.

question: Venezuela's hyperinflation under Maduro reached peak severity around 2018-2019. By 2024 prices were rising at:
answer: Several thousand percent per year at various points
choices: Several thousand percent per year at various points
Below 1% per year — Venezuelan stability
Exactly the same as the US at 2%
Around 5% per year — moderate inflation
context: Venezuela's bolivar has been redenominated multiple times. Total cumulative inflation since Maduro took power exceeds millions of percent. Many Venezuelans use US dollars informally. Food shortages, mass emigration, political repression — the predictable consequences of price controls plus money printing.

question: Why did the Hungarian forint replace the pengo in August 1946 after the worst hyperinflation in history?
answer: Only a brand-new currency with credible reform could break the inflation cycle.
choices: Only a brand-new currency with credible reform could break the inflation cycle.
The pengo was simply too pretty to keep using.
Hungary became a Soviet satellite state forcefully
The pengo had no actual paper production left.
context: Hungary's pengo had reached prices doubling every 15 hours. Inflation expectations had to be broken. The forint was introduced with stricter monetary discipline. Inflation stabilized. The pattern (new currency + credible reform) repeats: Israeli shekel (1985), Brazilian real (1994), Argentine peso (1991, until 2001).

question: Why does the 'Cantillon effect' explain why newly created money helps some people more than others?
answer: Those who receive new money first can spend at old prices before prices rise.
choices: Those who receive new money first can spend at old prices before prices rise.
All citizens benefit equally from any money printing
Newly printed money disappears immediately without effect
Money creation is impossible in modern economies.
context: Richard Cantillon's 18th-century insight. The banker, the government contractor, the bondholder get the new money first. They spend at pre-inflation prices. By the time the money reaches workers and savers, prices have already risen. Inflation isn't neutral — it redistributes from late receivers to early receivers.

question: Why did the US 'transitory' inflation framing of 2021 fail so badly?
answer: Massive money printing combined with broken supply chains drove sustained inflation
choices: Massive money printing combined with broken supply chains drove sustained inflation
Inflation actually was temporary as predicted by the Fed.
Inflation was caused only by gas prices that year.
There was no real inflation in the US in 2021.
context: Powell, Yellen, and others called rising prices 'transitory' through November 2021. By then CPI was 6.8%. June 2022 peak: 9.1% — highest since November 1981. The framing damaged Fed credibility. The lesson: don't dismiss inflation when fiscal and monetary expansion has been historic.

question: The Federal Reserve's response to 2021-22 inflation included the most aggressive rate-hike cycle since when?
answer: Volcker's 1979-82 cycle
choices: Volcker's 1979-82 cycle
Burns's 1970s cycle
Bernanke's 2004-07 cycle
Greenspan's 1994 cycle
context: 0% to 5.5% in 16 months — fastest absolute change since Volcker. Burns let inflation get away. Bernanke's was a slow normalization. Powell had to catch up after months of denial. The 2022-23 cycle's success or failure is still being debated, but it was historically aggressive.

question: Why does Modern Monetary Theory (MMT) face strong empirical objections after the 2021-23 inflation episode?
answer: MMT's prediction that deficit spending wouldn't cause inflation was falsified.
choices: MMT's prediction that deficit spending wouldn't cause inflation was falsified.
MMT was actually proven right by the inflation that occurred.
MMT had never made any specific predictions to test.
MMT was never actually implemented anywhere ever.
context: Stephanie Kelton's 'The Deficit Myth' (2020) predicted no inflation from COVID stimulus. Inflation followed. MMT advocates argue the wrong tax-spending mix or supply shocks. Critics call this unfalsifiable goalpost-moving. The basic claim — currency issuers face no nominal constraint up to full employment — is empirically problematic.

question: Why is gold's modern price rise (~$280 in 2000 to ~$2400 in 2024) cited as evidence of fiat money's weakness?
answer: Central banks expanded money supplies much faster than gold supply grew
choices: Central banks expanded money supplies much faster than gold supply grew
Gold actually fell against most major currencies during this time
Gold rose because of new industrial uses for the metal
Gold rose because more jewelry was being purchased annually.
context: Volcker discipline gave way. QE, ZIRP, post-2020 stimulus — all drove hard-asset bids. Gold and Bitcoin both serve as escape valves from fiat debasement. The gold rise tracks the M2 expansion across major currencies. Sound-money critics see this as confirmation of fiat's gradual failure.

question: David Ricardo's 1817 'Principles' used a famous example to show that even a country worse at everything still gains from trade. What was the example?
answer: England and Portugal trading cloth and wine
choices: England and Portugal trading cloth and wine
France and Spain trading wheat and beef
Germany and Italy trading steel and cars
US and Mexico trading corn and oil
context: Ricardo: Portugal could produce both cloth and wine more efficiently than England. Yet both gain by Portugal specializing in wine and England in cloth — because Portugal's relative cost differs. Comparative advantage. The deepest insight in trade theory. Counterintuitive but rock-solid.

question: Why is comparative advantage often called the most counterintuitive idea in economics?
answer: Even a country worse at everything still benefits from specializing
choices: Even a country worse at everything still benefits from specializing
It is the same as absolute advantage.
It applies only to countries the same size
It works only when one country dominates
context: Most people think a country has to be 'best' at something to gain. Ricardo proved otherwise. Even the worst country at everything has SOME relative strength. Both sides gain. The principle defends free trade against every protectionist argument from the 1800s to today.

question: Why do most economists oppose tariffs even when they 'protect' domestic industries?
answer: Tariffs help one industry at the cost of consumers and other industries
choices: Tariffs help one industry at the cost of consumers and other industries
Tariffs always make foreign goods cheaper for buyers
Tariffs are forbidden under the US Constitution.
Tariffs make domestic industries fail faster
context: Steel tariffs help steel makers; hurt steel buyers (auto makers, construction). The cost to many far exceeds the gain to few. Studies of Trump-era and Biden-era tariffs confirm. The Cantillon-like distribution rewards politically-connected industries. Both parties keep using them.

question: Why has the WTO (World Trade Organization, founded 1995) faced declining influence in recent years?
answer: Major powers have increasingly used tariffs and trade restrictions unilaterally.
choices: Major powers have increasingly used tariffs and trade restrictions unilaterally.
The WTO became too powerful for any country to challenge
All trade disputes were resolved permanently by 2010.
The WTO ran out of money and shut down operations.
context: US-China trade war (2018-), industrial policy revival, national-security exceptions, post-COVID supply concerns — all have eroded WTO authority. The dispute settlement system has been crippled by US blocking appellate body appointments. Economic nationalism has returned in both parties.

question: Why are 'comparative advantage' and 'absolute advantage' different concepts in trade theory?
answer: Comparative: relative opportunity cost; Absolute: actual production cost
choices: Comparative: relative opportunity cost; Absolute: actual production cost
Comparative and absolute are exactly the same concept.
Comparative applies to goods; absolute to services
Comparative is for big countries; absolute is for small.
context: Absolute advantage = you produce faster/cheaper than them. Comparative = you produce A at lower opportunity cost than B. The crucial insight: comparative advantage matters even when one party has absolute advantage in everything. Trade always benefits both sides. This is settled microeconomic theory.

question: If your phone bill goes up by 5% each year, in 14 years it will roughly:
answer: Double from where it started
choices: Double from where it started
Stay exactly the same
Drop by half each year
Triple within five years
context: The Rule of 72: 72 / 5 = ~14 years to double at 5% inflation. Bills, rents, and groceries follow the same math. Compounding works for and against you over decades.

question: Why do most stores accept cards even when they pay 2-3% in fees to card companies?
answer: Card buyers spend more than cash buyers usually do.
choices: Card buyers spend more than cash buyers usually do.
Stores must take all cards by US federal law.
Card companies pay stores extra each month
Cards stop all kinds of robbery at the door
context: Card fees hurt margins, but cash-only stores miss bigger purchases. Card buyers don't think as hard about spending. The net effect is usually positive for sellers. Some small stores still go cash-only to save the fee.

question: Why does the price of a single Bitcoin go up and down so much in a week?
answer: It's a small market with no government backing the price
choices: It's a small market with no government backing the price
Banks set the Bitcoin price each morning
Bitcoin's price is locked in by the SEC.
Bitcoin only changes price on weekends
context: Bitcoin's market cap is large but still small compared to gold or major currencies. Big buyers or sellers can move the price quickly. Sentiment, news, and ETF flows all add volatility. Long-term holders ignore daily moves.

question: Why does a new car lose about 20% of its value the moment you drive it off the lot?
answer: Buyers know it's used now; resellers must offer less.
choices: Buyers know it's used now; resellers must offer less.
Cars get heavier after they leave the lot
All car prices fall by 20% every Sunday
Cars are required to lose value by law.
context: A 'new' car becomes a 'used' car the second it leaves. Insurance, history, and unknowns drop the resale price fast. Many financial writers say to buy 1-2 year old used cars to avoid this depreciation hit.

question: Why is buying a house often called 'the biggest purchase of your life'?
answer: Homes typically cost 3-5 times yearly household income
choices: Homes typically cost 3-5 times yearly household income
Houses are the only thing you can ever own.
Houses are heavier than any other purchase.
House prices are picked by the city mayor.
context: Median US home: ~$400K. Median household income: ~$75K. The mortgage often runs 30 years. Saving for a down payment takes years. The choice deserves careful thought — but most people get little training on it.

question: Why do landlords sometimes prefer steady tenants over higher-paying short-term ones?
answer: Less risk of empty months and lower turnover costs
choices: Less risk of empty months and lower turnover costs
Steady tenants always pay double the rent
Landlords must take long-term tenants by law.
Short-term tenants always damage the home
context: Empty months kill landlord cash flow. New tenants need cleaning, painting, listing fees. A steady $1500 tenant beats a $1800 tenant with frequent turnover. Stability has real value beyond the monthly check.

question: Why does the US Treasury sell bonds to the public?
answer: To borrow money for spending beyond what taxes cover
choices: To borrow money for spending beyond what taxes cover
To give free money to American citizens
Because banks need bonds to make pencils
Bonds are the only legal way to pay taxes.
context: When Congress spends more than it collects, the Treasury borrows the gap. Treasuries are sold weekly at auction. Foreign and domestic buyers hold $27T+ in US debt. Interest on the debt is now over $1T/year.

question: Why do credit card companies sometimes offer 0% interest 'introductory' rates?
answer: To attract new customers who often pay regular rates later
choices: To attract new customers who often pay regular rates later
Because the cards cost nothing to make
Because credit cards are illegal otherwise.
Because the banks like generous gifts
context: 0% intro rates are loss leaders. Many users don't pay off during the intro period, then face 20-30% rates. The cards earn from those who slide into balance debt. Use them strategically; don't get trapped.

question: Why do supermarket prices change so often on items like meat, eggs, and produce?
answer: Wholesale costs and supply shift weekly with farm conditions
choices: Wholesale costs and supply shift weekly with farm conditions
Stores enjoy printing new tags every Sunday
Prices are set by the city's mayor each week.
Items get heavier when prices stay the same
context: Bird flu shrinks egg supply; eggs spike. Drought hits corn; meat prices rise. Stores get new wholesale prices weekly. They pass cost changes through. Bread, milk, and eggs are most volatile because they're tied to short supply chains.

question: Why is 'opportunity cost' so important to think about even for simple choices?
answer: Every choice closes off other options that had value too.
choices: Every choice closes off other options that had value too.
Costs always show up only on receipts you keep
Choices are the same as random guesses always.
Opportunity is bought directly with money.
context: Going to a 2-hour movie means not doing 2 hours of something else. Buying a $50 dinner is also $50 not invested. The 'cost' of an action includes what you give up — not just what you pay. The hardest economic idea to keep in mind.

question: Why do most rich Americans pay a lower effective tax rate than middle-income workers?
answer: Income comes from capital gains and dividends, taxed lower than wages
choices: Income comes from capital gains and dividends, taxed lower than wages
Rich people don't pay any tax at all in America
The IRS gives rich Americans a free pass
All Americans pay the exact same tax rate
context: Long-term capital gains: max 20%. Top wage rate: 37%. Plus payroll tax on wages. Buffett famously pays a lower rate than his secretary. Critics say tax this. Defenders say capital is taxed already at the corporate level. The debate goes on.

question: Why is a 'recession' often hard to define exactly until after it's over?
answer: It usually needs two quarters of falling GDP, but other signs matter too
choices: It usually needs two quarters of falling GDP, but other signs matter too
Recessions only happen in the middle of summer
All economists agree on the same definition daily
Recessions are picked by a private committee.
context: The NBER's Business Cycle Dating Committee declares recessions. They use jobs, GDP, income, sales — multiple indicators. The 'two quarters of falling GDP' rule is a shorthand, not the official definition. Recessions are often called only months after they start.

question: Why is Friedrich Hayek considered one of the 20th century's most influential economists despite being out of fashion mid-career?
answer: He outlived his critics and lived to see his ideas vindicated.
choices: He outlived his critics and lived to see his ideas vindicated.
He invented modern macroeconomic policy in 1944.
He won every prize given to any economist before 1990.
He was the first central banker in the world.
context: Hayek (1899-1992) was sidelined by Keynesians from the 1940s to the 1970s. Stagflation broke that consensus. He won the 1974 Nobel. By 1992 he had seen the Berlin Wall fall and the Soviet collapse — vindication of his core claims about central planning.

question: Why is the term 'malinvestment' central to Austrian Business Cycle Theory?
answer: Cheap credit lures firms to build projects that fail when rates normalize
choices: Cheap credit lures firms to build projects that fail when rates normalize
Investors always make mistakes about all stocks always
Government investments always lose money quickly
All investments are mistakes during recessions.
context: Mises and Hayek's theory: when central banks push rates below natural levels, firms over-build long-horizon assets (housing, factories, tech). The bust is the inevitable correction. The 2000 and 2008 crashes both fit this pattern. ABCT predicted what mainstream macro missed.

question: Why does the term 'Cantillon effect' name a hidden cost of money printing?
answer: Those nearest the new money spend at old prices before they rise
choices: Those nearest the new money spend at old prices before they rise
Cantillon's effect makes all prices fall equally
Cantillon's effect helps poor people the most
Cantillon's effect prevents inflation entirely
context: Richard Cantillon's 1730 observation. New money reaches bankers, government contractors, bond dealers first. They spend at pre-inflation prices. By the time the money reaches workers and savers, prices have already risen. Inflation isn't neutral — it redistributes wealth toward the early receivers.

question: Why did the 2008-09 crisis lead to massive Fed balance-sheet expansion?
answer: Bernanke applied lessons from the Great Depression to avoid deflation
choices: Bernanke applied lessons from the Great Depression to avoid deflation
Banks demanded the Fed buy their stocks directly
The 2008 crisis was actually a banking holiday plan.
Congress required the Fed to triple its balance sheet
context: Bernanke was a Great Depression scholar. His core lesson: don't let the money supply collapse. QE1, QE2, QE3 expanded the Fed's balance sheet from $900B to $4.5T. Critics on the right say QE bailed out asset holders. Defenders say it averted a depression.

question: Why is 'too big to fail' considered a serious problem in modern banking?
answer: Big banks know they'll be bailed out, encouraging more risk.
choices: Big banks know they'll be bailed out, encouraging more risk.
Big banks are required to be small by law.
Big banks are too small to fail in any way.
Big banks pay extra taxes to compensate
context: Heads I win, tails taxpayers lose. The 2008 bailouts of major banks set a precedent. Dodd-Frank tried to address it. The 2023 SVB rescue extended even to deposits above the $250K limit. Critics on both left and right call TBTF the root of moral hazard.

question: Why is Buchanan and Tullock's 'Calculus of Consent' considered foundational to public choice theory?
answer: It applies economic logic to political behavior systematically
choices: It applies economic logic to political behavior systematically
It explained how to balance the federal budget
It proved socialism is better than capitalism.
It calculated voter consent mathematically
context: Their 1962 book treated politicians and voters as self-interested like consumers. The implications: many 'government failures' are predictable, not accidents. Buchanan won the 1986 Nobel. The field has grown enormously since.

question: Why does Mancur Olson's 'Logic of Collective Action' explain why small interest groups often win?
answer: Small groups can monitor members; large groups face free-rider problems.
choices: Small groups can monitor members; large groups face free-rider problems.
Large groups always win in any democratic process
Small groups have less money than larger groups.
All groups face exactly the same coordination cost
context: Olson's 1965 book. Each sugar farmer cares about tariffs; each shopper barely notices. Sugar farmers organize and lobby; shoppers don't. Asymmetric organization beats asymmetric numbers. The pattern explains farm subsidies, occupational licensing, urban zoning, tariffs.

question: Why are 'iron triangles' a problem in US politics?
answer: Agency, lobby, and committee work together against the public interest
choices: Agency, lobby, and committee work together against the public interest
Iron is a heavy metal that locks votes in place.
Triangles are stable shapes that hold all weight.
Iron triangles only exist in foreign countries
context: Classic example: defense contractors, the Pentagon, and the armed services committees. They serve each other and resist outside reform. Same pattern in agriculture (USDA, farm lobby, ag committee). Hard to break; built into the structure of government.

question: Why did Argentina default on $93 billion of sovereign debt in 2001?
answer: The peso-dollar peg became unsustainable after years of fiscal deficits
choices: The peso-dollar peg became unsustainable after years of fiscal deficits
Foreign nations refused to lend Argentina any money
Argentina was conquered by neighboring countries.
Argentina was the only country to never default.
context: Five presidents in two weeks. Deposits frozen (corralito). Peso devalued from 1:1 to 4:1 within months. The default ended Convertibility. Argentina has since defaulted again multiple times. The pattern: deficits + fixed exchange rate + political weakness = crisis.

question: Why did Lebanon's banking system collapse beginning in October 2019?
answer: Banks had paid impossibly high dollar interest funded by new dollar inflows.
choices: Banks had paid impossibly high dollar interest funded by new dollar inflows.
An earthquake destroyed all Lebanese banks.
The US placed military sanctions on Lebanese banks
All Lebanese citizens stopped using money
context: Riad Salameh ran the Banque du Liban for 30 years. The Ponzi-like scheme paid 10%+ on dollar deposits funded by ever more inflows. When inflows stopped, depositors lost most of their savings. The lira lost 98% of value. Hyperinflation followed. A Madoff at the national scale.

question: Why is the 1907 Panic considered the most important banking crisis in US history?
answer: It led directly to the creation of the Federal Reserve in 1913.
choices: It led directly to the creation of the Federal Reserve in 1913.
It was the smallest crisis in US banking history.
It was solved entirely by Congress in three days.
It happened during a period of stable banking
context: Morgan's private rescue from his library showed the US needed an institution. The 'next time we may not have Morgan' argument won. The National Monetary Commission's recommendations led through Jekyll Island (1910) to the Federal Reserve Act (1913).

question: Why did Britain leave the gold standard in 1931 after returning in 1925?
answer: The pre-war parity proved unsustainable in deflationary postwar conditions
choices: The pre-war parity proved unsustainable in deflationary postwar conditions
Britain had no more gold left in any reserves.
All foreign nations forced Britain to abandon gold
Britain decided gold standards were too easy to maintain.
context: Churchill, as Chancellor in 1925, returned at pre-war parity over Keynes's objections. The overvalued pound crushed exports. In September 1931, after years of pressure, Britain left. A wave of competitive devaluations followed. The interwar gold standard was over.

question: Why is 'fractional reserve banking' controversial among Austrian economists?
answer: Banks lend out most deposits, multiplying credit beyond the initial deposit
choices: Banks lend out most deposits, multiplying credit beyond the initial deposit
Banks must keep 100% reserves by Austrian law.
Fractional reserves are universally accepted as fine.
Fractional reserve banking is illegal in most US states.
context: If 10% reserve required, a $100 deposit can support $1000 of loans. Critics (Huerta de Soto especially) say this is fraud and the source of business cycles. Defenders say it efficiently intermediates between savers and borrowers. Both positions have intellectual roots in Austrian thought.

question: Why did Mises predict in 1920 that socialism would fail economically?
answer: Without market prices, planners can't tell what's scarce or what to make
choices: Without market prices, planners can't tell what's scarce or what to make
Socialist workers were too lazy to make any goods.
Socialist countries had no resources for production.
Socialism was outlawed in all 20th-century countries.
context: Mises's 'calculation problem': a planner deciding between steel-for-cars or steel-for-houses has no price signal. They guess. The USSR ran on guesswork for 70 years and finally collapsed. Hayek extended the argument to information generally — knowledge is dispersed; no planner has it all.

question: Why did Mises and Hayek warn against 'rationalist constructivism' in social institutions?
answer: Institutions evolved over centuries; reformers usually destroy more than they build
choices: Institutions evolved over centuries; reformers usually destroy more than they build
All institutions should be designed by central planners.
Markets are rationally constructed by experts.
Tradition is always inferior to fresh thinking.
context: Hayek's 1988 'The Fatal Conceit' is the canonical text. The 'conceit' is thinking we can design society better than what trial-and-error over millennia produced. Markets, common law, family, tradition — each evolved without designers. Burn it down and you lose what works.

question: Why does Israel Kirzner emphasize 'alertness' rather than 'risk-taking' in entrepreneurship?
answer: Entrepreneurs notice unmet needs others miss, not just bet on uncertainty
choices: Entrepreneurs notice unmet needs others miss, not just bet on uncertainty
Alertness is the same thing as risk-taking exactly.
Risk-taking is illegal in modern economies.
Entrepreneurs do not exist in real markets.
context: Kirzner (1973): the entrepreneur isn't a daredevil but an observer. A $5 car wash where neighboring towns charge $15. Alertness, not gambling. Markets are constantly in disequilibrium; entrepreneurs close the gaps. Closer to Mengerian roots than Schumpeter's 'creative destruction.'

question: Why did Joseph Schumpeter call market dynamism 'creative destruction'?
answer: Innovation continuously destroys existing positions to create new ones
choices: Innovation continuously destroys existing positions to create new ones
Creative destruction means random damage to businesses
Destruction is the only thing markets ever do.
Creative people destroy everything in their path
context: AT&T's long-distance monopoly destroyed by VoIP. Kodak by digital. Blockbuster by Netflix. The dynamic Austrian-Schumpeterian view says monopolies are temporary unless protected by government. Static-equilibrium analysis (used in mainstream antitrust) misses this.

question: Why did Henry Ford's 1914 $5 wage cause both praise and criticism?
answer: It doubled going rates, but smaller firms couldn't match it
choices: It doubled going rates, but smaller firms couldn't match it
The Ford wage was illegal under American labor laws.
All US factories adopted the same wage in that year
The wage was actually below the market rate that year.
context: Ford's mass production made $5/day economically viable; smaller factories couldn't match. Critics: not all firms can pay above-market wages. Defenders: Ford showed that high wages plus high productivity can be a virtuous cycle. The debate continues today.

question: Why did Jack Bogle's index funds revolutionize retail investing despite being initially mocked?
answer: Decades of data showed most active managers underperform after fees.
choices: Decades of data showed most active managers underperform after fees.
Bogle's funds promised guaranteed returns higher than stocks
Index funds were required by law to be low fee.
Active managers all banded together to fight Bogle
context: Bogle's First Index Investment Trust (1976) was called 'Bogle's Folly.' Today index funds dominate retail. Even Warren Buffett recommends them for non-pros. Bogle saved retail investors trillions in fees over decades. He died 2019 having reshaped how Americans invest.

question: Why did Warren Buffett bet against hedge funds for ten years (2008-2017)?
answer: He believed index funds would beat hedge funds after fees.
choices: He believed index funds would beat hedge funds after fees.
He owned all the hedge funds in America
He had personal grudges with hedge fund managers.
Buffett ran a hedge fund of his own at the time.
context: Buffett's S&P 500 fund returned 7.1%/year; the hedge funds returned 2.2%. The $1M went to Girls Inc. of Omaha. A vivid lesson in passive investing. Buffett's 2017 letter detailed how fees ate hedge fund returns. The bet became iconic in finance circles.

question: Why does the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) require companies to publish quarterly financials?
answer: To give all investors equal access to material information
choices: To give all investors equal access to material information
To raise the most tax revenue for the government
Because the SEC enjoys reading the reports
It is required by international law worldwide.
context: 10-Q (quarterly) and 10-K (annual) filings. The principle: no insider should know more than ordinary buyers. Created after 1933-34 reforms following the 1929 crash. The system isn't perfect (Enron, FTX) but it makes markets generally trustworthy.

question: Why do antitrust laws sometimes lead to ironic outcomes?
answer: Trustbusters can break up the very firms creating consumer benefits.
choices: Trustbusters can break up the very firms creating consumer benefits.
Antitrust always helps consumers in every case
Antitrust laws are never actually enforced.
All firms benefit from antitrust enforcement
context: Standard Oil's breakup (1911) helped some consumers. Microsoft's antitrust battles (1998-2001) arguably helped no one. Amazon, Google, Apple now face actions. Critics: antitrust often serves rivals, not consumers. Defenders: market power is real and must be policed. Both have evidence.

question: Why did the 2017 ICO boom and bust become a defining case for crypto skepticism?
answer: Studies showed 78-92% of ICOs were scams or failed to deliver.
choices: Studies showed 78-92% of ICOs were scams or failed to deliver.
ICOs were all successful businesses by 2020.
ICOs were created by the US government.
All ICOs returned investor money in full
context: $5.6 billion raised; vast majority gone. SEC enforcement followed. The episode left a generation of retail investors burned. Bitcoin maximalists use it as evidence that Bitcoin is fundamentally different from the broader 'crypto' space. The track record speaks for itself.

question: Why was Sam Bankman-Fried's effective altruism connection significant?
answer: EA leaders had championed him; the fraud damaged the movement.
choices: EA leaders had championed him; the fraud damaged the movement.
EA is the same thing as Effective Action politically.
EA is a Bitcoin-related programming language.
EA had refused all FTX donations from SBF.
context: SBF positioned himself as an EA hero — making billions to give away. Major EA figures praised him. The 2022 collapse and 2023 conviction were a body blow to EA's credibility. Critics: utilitarian end-justifies-means logic enabled the fraud. The movement is still recovering.

question: Why did the Terra/Luna stablecoin collapse in May 2022 wipe out tens of billions?
answer: Its 'stable' value relied on a separate coin that crashed
choices: Its 'stable' value relied on a separate coin that crashed
Terra was hacked by foreign government agents.
All Terra users withdrew their coins at once
Terra was outlawed in every major country.
context: Terra's UST stablecoin was 'backed' by Luna — but Luna's price relied on faith in UST. When the loop broke, both crashed to near zero. $40B+ vaporized. The Korean founder, Do Kwon, was arrested in Montenegro on a forged passport. Algorithmic stablecoins fell out of fashion.

question: Why is Hong Kong's currency board considered a 'monetary discipline' experiment?
answer: Every HK dollar must be backed by US dollar reserves at a fixed rate.
choices: Every HK dollar must be backed by US dollar reserves at a fixed rate.
Hong Kong banks all use Bitcoin as reserves
Hong Kong uses no money at all in business
Hong Kong prints US dollars officially each year
context: Since 1983, the HKMA holds USD reserves equal to HKD in circulation. The peg has survived 1997, 2008, 2020 — but Hong Kong imports US monetary policy with no say. Trade-off: stability vs. local control. A working example of currency board discipline.

question: Why did Estonia's post-1992 currency board succeed where many post-Soviet currencies failed?
answer: Strict discipline plus a brand-new currency backed by Deutsche Marks
choices: Strict discipline plus a brand-new currency backed by Deutsche Marks
Estonia was the largest post-Soviet country.
Estonia had no economic ties with Russia.
Estonia was given free dollars by the IMF.
context: PM Mart Laar (a young Friedman reader) introduced a DM-backed kroon in 1992. Inflation broke. Estonia became the EU's most digital and free-market member. Joined the euro in 2011. The Baltic states are textbook cases of how monetary discipline anchors broader economic reform.

question: Why did Panama dollarize in 1904 instead of issuing its own paper currency?
answer: Dollar parity after Colombia independence gave instant stability.
choices: Dollar parity after Colombia independence gave instant stability.
Panama was a US territory until the 1990s.
Panama is too small to print its own money.
Panama joined the Federal Reserve at founding
context: Panama prints no paper currency of its own. Coins are minted locally; bills are US dollars. Inflation rates have tracked the US closely. The arrangement preceded modern dollarization theory — a century-long natural experiment in monetary discipline.

question: Why is Switzerland's franc considered a 'safe haven' currency?
answer: Long political stability plus disciplined central banking
choices: Long political stability plus disciplined central banking
Switzerland has the world's largest gold reserves.
Swiss banks pay the highest interest rates globally
Swiss francs are the only currency made of gold.
context: When global risks rise, money flows into CHF. The Swiss National Bank has historically been disciplined. In 2015 the SNB abandoned the EUR peg, sending the franc soaring 20% in a day. The episode showed even safe-haven currencies face limits. CHF remains a port in storms.

question: Why is the 2008-09 housing crisis cited as a textbook example of moral hazard?
answer: Banks had every reason to make risky loans expecting bailout.
choices: Banks had every reason to make risky loans expecting bailout.
Banks were never bailed out during the crisis.
Moral hazard doesn't apply to housing markets
Banks all refused government help that year
context: Subprime mortgages, NINJA loans, packaged into AAA-rated MBS. When prices fell, the system unraveled. Bear, Lehman, AIG, the auto bailouts — the precedent was set. Banks knew the next crisis would also be backstopped. The 2023 SVB rescue confirmed the pattern.

question: Why does the 2008 GFC mark a turning point in central bank power?
answer: Fed, ECB, BoE, BoJ all began direct asset buying at new scale
choices: Fed, ECB, BoE, BoJ all began direct asset buying at new scale
Central banks were abolished after the global crisis.
All central banks shrank during the global crisis
Only the US Federal Reserve responded to the crisis
context: QE 1, 2, 3 globally. Negative rates in Europe and Japan. Direct asset purchases at unprecedented scale. The 'unconventional' became conventional. Critics argue central banks are now central planners.

question: Why did the Iceland banking collapse of 2008 force the country to default?
answer: Bank assets had grown to ten times national GDP.
choices: Bank assets had grown to ten times national GDP.
Iceland refused to bail out its banks for fun
Iceland was conquered by Britain that year.
Iceland had no banks before the 2008 crisis.
context: Glitnir, Landsbanki, Kaupthing — combined assets 10x Icelandic GDP. They had borrowed dollars and euros heavily. When the GFC froze interbank lending, no central bank could rescue them. Iceland defaulted, devalued, restructured.

question: Why is Bastiat's broken-window fallacy still relevant today?
answer: Politicians regularly claim disasters or wars stimulate the economy
choices: Politicians regularly claim disasters or wars stimulate the economy
Bastiat lived in the 21st century recently.
Broken windows are a major US tax issue today.
The fallacy was proven correct by Keynes.
context: After 9/11, Paul Krugman wrote that the destruction might stimulate growth. The WWII-ended-the-Depression myth persists. Cash-for-clunkers paid people to destroy working cars. Each episode revives the broken window fallacy. Bastiat's reply: what is unseen is the foregone investment.

question: Why does the 'seen and unseen' framework apply to government spending?
answer: Visible benefits get attention; foregone alternatives don't
choices: Visible benefits get attention; foregone alternatives don't
Government spending is always seen by all.
The unseen never matters in policy debates
Government can spend without any opportunity cost.
context: A new federal program creates visible jobs. Less visible: the higher taxes or borrowing that pays for it, the private spending that would have happened instead. Bastiat's framework defeats much political rhetoric. Hazlitt's 'Economics in One Lesson' (1946) extended it.

question: Why does the labor theory of value fail to explain modern prices?
answer: Hours of labor don't determine what buyers will pay.
choices: Hours of labor don't determine what buyers will pay.
All goods take the same labor to make
Labor is the only cost of any product.
Marx never made claims about value at all.
context: Menger demolished the labor theory in 1871. Bohm-Bawerk's 1896 essay closed the door on Marx's economics. The price of a thing depends on subjective demand and marginal utility — not on production cost or labor hours. A diamond pendant takes less labor than digging a ditch.

question: Why is 'subjective value' considered a foundational insight of modern economics?
answer: Value lives in the mind of the buyer, not in the object
choices: Value lives in the mind of the buyer, not in the object
All value is decided by the government always.
Objects have an objective true intrinsic value.
Subjective value is the same as labor theory.
context: Menger's 1871 'Principles' overturned classical economics. A diamond is worth more than water in town; on a desert island, water wins. Value is ranked by individuals making choices. Mainstream economics absorbed this. Austrian economics emphasizes it most strongly.

question: Why does 'marginal' analysis matter so much in microeconomics?
answer: Decisions are made at the margin — one more or one less.
choices: Decisions are made at the margin — one more or one less.
All economic choices are huge yes-no decisions.
Marginal means the same as average always
Marginal analysis was invented in the 1990s.
context: The diamond-water paradox: water has higher TOTAL utility, but at the margin, your next glass of water is worth less than your next diamond. Modern economics is largely an extension of marginal analysis. Most policy debates make sense only when framed at the margin.

question: Why is the gold standard considered to have ended in 1971 rather than 1933 or 1944?
answer: Nixon closed the gold window for foreign central banks
choices: Nixon closed the gold window for foreign central banks
Gold became completely illegal worldwide in 1971
All US gold was destroyed by Congress in 1971.
Gold standards never actually existed at any time
context: 1933: FDR confiscated American gold. 1944: Bretton Woods kept the dollar at $35/oz for foreign central banks. 1971: Nixon shut even that down. Critics call this the founding moment of pure fiat. Defenders say the gold standard was already broken.

question: Why has the dollar lost about 96% of its purchasing power since the Federal Reserve was founded in 1913?
answer: Money expansion has outpaced economic growth most of those years.
choices: Money expansion has outpaced economic growth most of those years.
The dollar has actually gained value since 1913.
Gold prices rose 30 times since 1913 only
The Fed strictly preserved the dollar's value
context: $1 in 1913 buys what about $0.04 buys today. Over 110+ years, that's roughly 3% inflation per year compounded. Volcker's 1980s discipline didn't fully reverse the long trend. Critics blame the Fed; defenders argue mild inflation is healthy. The lost purchasing power is real either way.

question: Why is Adam Smith called the 'father of modern economics' even though he wasn't the first economist?
answer: Wealth of Nations (1776) systematically built an economic worldview.
choices: Wealth of Nations (1776) systematically built an economic worldview.
Smith was the first person to ever write about money.
Smith founded the first economics department.
Smith was the only economist before the 1800s.
context: Smith built on Aquinas, the Scholastics, Petty, Hume, the Physiocrats. His 1776 book synthesized and extended their work. Division of labor, the invisible hand, opposition to mercantilism — all systematized. The book launched modern economics as a discipline.

question: Why does Adam Smith's 'invisible hand' concept survive misunderstanding by both critics and admirers?
answer: Smith used the phrase only a few times across all his work
choices: Smith used the phrase only a few times across all his work
Smith never used the phrase at all in any writing
Smith repeated the phrase on every page
Smith invented the phrase to describe socialism.
context: The phrase appears three times: in History of Astronomy, in Theory of Moral Sentiments, in Wealth of Nations. Smith used it lightly. Modern enthusiasm has overstated his emphasis. Modern critics use it as a strawman. The concept survives because it captures real coordination.

question: Why is the 'self-interest' that Adam Smith described in Wealth of Nations often misunderstood?
answer: Smith wrote The Theory of Moral Sentiments first, showing humans have many motives.
choices: Smith wrote The Theory of Moral Sentiments first, showing humans have many motives.
Smith wrote only about money and greed in his books.
Smith was a Marxist who attacked self-interest entirely.
Smith was the same person as Karl Marx, just renamed.
context: Smith's 1759 'Theory of Moral Sentiments' is mostly about other motivations — sympathy, conscience, virtue. WoN (1776) showed self-interest harnessed by markets to social ends. The two books together form Smith's complete account. Many critics read only WoN — and only partial bits at that.

question: Why is the term 'invisible hand' a useful metaphor even after centuries?
answer: Markets produce ordered outcomes without anyone designing them
choices: Markets produce ordered outcomes without anyone designing them
There is a literal invisible hand that helps shoppers.
The invisible hand can be replaced by central planners.
The invisible hand is the same as government policy.
context: No central office plans how many shoes to make or who gets bread. Yet shoes get made and bread gets distributed. Prices and competition coordinate strangers. The metaphor of an 'invisible hand' captures emergent order from voluntary trade. Modern Austrians call it 'spontaneous order.'

question: Why are some workers harder to replace than others in the labor market?
answer: Rare skills draw a small pool; common skills draw many
choices: Rare skills draw a small pool; common skills draw many
All workers are equally easy or hard to replace.
Labor markets have no elasticity in any case.
Workers can never bargain over their wages.
context: A surgeon who is one of 10 in the world has high bargaining power. A burger flipper has many substitutes. This is why high-skill workers earn more than low-skill workers — supply and demand applied to labor.

question: Why did Ricardo's 1817 example of England and Portugal trading remain influential?
answer: Both gain by specializing even when one is better at all goods.
choices: Both gain by specializing even when one is better at all goods.
England and Portugal still trade only wine today
England never accepted Ricardo's trade theory
Portugal was actually worse at making both goods.
context: Ricardo's example: Portugal is better at both cloth and wine. England specializes in cloth; Portugal in wine. Both gain. The math is rock-solid. Trade always benefits both sides, even when one is absolutely better. The deepest insight in trade theory.
